t.navizarsah castle@36.4,50.7:
North of Qazvin, the Alborz mountains rise in a wall of bare, folded rock, and behind them lies the Alamut region, a tangle of valleys, gorges and crags that has a legend all of its own. In the late eleventh century, Hassan-i Sabbah, leader of the Nizari Ismailis, seized the castle of Alamut, and from it and a network of mountain strongholds his followers resisted the Seljuk sultans for generations. Western chroniclers later called them the Assassins and wove lurid tales around them. The Mongols under Hulagu finally took and slighted the castles in 1256. Navizaršāh is one of the fortified sites scattered through these mountains, and while its own history is little documented in sources most travellers can reach, its setting tells you everything about why people built strongholds here: high ground, hard access and long views over the valleys.

The landscape is stark and beautiful: red, ochre and grey rock, small green villages along the rivers, terraces of walnut and cherry trees, and snow on the peaks until late spring. The Alamut valley is popular with hikers and climbers, and the villages offer simple guesthouses, where you can sleep on carpets and eat home-cooked food.

Riding in Iran requires careful preparation. Rules for motorcycles, especially larger bikes and foreign-registered vehicles, are strict and can change, and you will need the right documents to bring a vehicle into the country. Check the current situation and official travel advice before planning a trip. The road from Qazvin over the mountains into the Alamut valley is spectacular, with hairpins, steep climbs and views, but the surface can be rough, with potholes, gravel and rockfalls, and local driving is unpredictable. The weather is extreme: hot summers in the lowlands, cold winters with snow in the mountains.

Services are limited in the mountains. Ābyek, about forty kilometres away, is the nearest town listed with full services, and Qazvin, a historic city with a fine bazaar and palaces from its time as Safavid capital, has everything. Fuel is cheap, but stations in remote areas are few, so carry extra. Try dizi, a lamb and chickpea stew cooked in a clay pot, and drink plenty of tea, offered everywhere as a sign of hospitality.
t.qostinlar fortification@36.4,50.3:
North of Qazvin, the Alborz mountains rise in a wall of rock between the Iranian plateau and the Caspian Sea, and in their valleys, a thousand years ago, a sect of Nizari Ismailis, known in the West as the Assassins, built a network of castles on mountaintops. The most famous, Alamut, was the base of Hassan-i Sabbah, the founder of the order, who captured it in 1090. The Qostinlar fortification is one of the lesser-known strongholds in the region, part of a system of castles and watchtowers that defended the valleys.

The Nizari Ismailis were a branch of Shia Islam, and they held their castles for over a century and a half, resisting the Seljuk sultans and gaining a reputation for targeted killings of their enemies, which gave rise to the legends of the Assassins. The Mongols destroyed their castles in 1256. Today the ruins are scattered on rocky peaks above the valleys, and Alamut itself, on a steep rock, is reached by a long climb on foot. The landscape is wild and beautiful, with deep gorges, rivers and terraced fields.

Riding to the Alamut valley from Qazvin means crossing a mountain pass on a winding road, with tight bends and steep gradients, and views back over the plain. The roads have improved in recent years, but surfaces can still be rough in places, and landslides and rockfalls can occur. The climate in the mountains is cooler than on the plain, with snow in winter. Foreign travellers in Iran face particular requirements, including visas and, for vehicles, a Carnet de Passages, and the situation for visitors can change, so check current advice before planning a trip.

Qazvin, about twenty-eight kilometres away, is a city of three hundred thousand with fuel and all services. Fuel in Iran has long been very cheap. The villages in the Alamut valley have basic services and guesthouses. Persian food is a delight: kebabs, rice dishes, stews such as ghormeh sabzi, and fresh bread. Iranian hospitality is famous, and travellers are often invited for tea. Standing among the ruins of an Assassin castle, with the mountains all around and the valley far below, is an experience you will not forget.
t.segment rio de la sal pampa del inca@-26:
Out here the Incas walked a road through country that most of us would call empty, and they did it without wheels, horses or a single petrol station. The stretch between the Río de la Sal and the Pampa del Inca is one of the Chilean pieces of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great Andean road network that tied Cusco to the far corners of the empire and was listed by UNESCO across six countries in 2014. In the Atacama region it shows up as a faint, dead-straight trace across gravel plains, sometimes edged with stones, sometimes marked by the low ruins of a tambo where runners and caravans once rested.

The nearest real town is Diego de Almagro, about 34 kilometres away, a mining town that grew up around copper and the railway, and it is where you sort out petrol, water and something to eat before heading into the open. Treat that as non-negotiable. Beyond it there is nothing commercial, no shade worth the name and no phone signal you should count on. Carry more water than seems sensible and tell someone where you are going.

The riding is about space rather than corners. Roads in this part of the desert are a mix of good tarmac laid for the mines and long gravel tracks where washboard ripples and soft patches of sand will test your arms and your patience. Wind gets up in the afternoon and comes across the pampa in hard gusts, so a morning run is kinder, and the low sun then throws long shadows that make the old road easier to pick out. Trucks serving the mines are big and fast; give them room and expect a wall of dust after each one.

What you get in return is light. The Atacama is one of the driest places on earth, and the air is so clear that hills thirty kilometres off look close enough to walk to. Colours change through the day from bleached grey to ochre, rust and violet, and after dark the sky is the reason observatories were built in this desert at all. The Río Salado, which gives the area its salty name, is a thin green line in an otherwise mineral world.

Stand on the old trace for a minute and think about the messengers who ran it in relays. Then get back on the bike, check your fuel gauge honestly, and head for Diego de Almagro with a margin to spare.
t.lambesar castle@36.5,50.2:
High in the Alborz mountains north of Qazvin, on a rocky spur above the Alamut valley, stand the remains of Lambsar, one of the strongest of the castles held by the Nizari Ismailis in the Middle Ages. To most Europeans this sect is known through the legend of the Assassins, a name that comes from distorted crusader and Persian tales. The reality was a network of mountain fortresses across Persia and Syria, ruled from Alamut, which resisted the Seljuk Turks and later the Mongols for over a century and a half.

Lambsar was taken by the Ismailis in the early twelfth century and became a key part of their defences in the region. When Hulagu Khan's Mongol armies arrived in the 1250s, most of the castles surrendered with their leader, but Lambsar is recorded as holding out for about a year longer, until disease weakened the garrison. Today the ruins are scattered on top of a steep crag, with remnants of walls, cisterns and storerooms cut into the rock. Reaching them requires a climb on foot, and the views over the valley and the mountains are spectacular.

The landscape is wild and beautiful. The Alamut region is a series of high valleys between the Alborz ranges, with rivers, orchards, terraced fields and villages of mud-brick houses. In spring the slopes turn green and the almond and walnut trees blossom; in winter, snow covers the passes. The air is clean, the light is sharp, and the silence is profound.

Riding here is an adventure. The road from Qazvin climbs over a high pass in the Alborz, with hairpins, steep gradients and long, dizzying drops, before descending into the Alamut valley. Surfaces vary from good asphalt to rough, broken sections, and landslides can block the road after heavy rain. Traffic is light, but trucks and local cars can appear suddenly on blind bends.

Practically, Qazvin is the nearest city with reliable fuel, food and accommodation; it is also an attractive place, with a fine bazaar and old mosques. In the valley, villages have small shops and simple guesthouses. Riding a motorcycle in Iran as a foreigner requires careful planning: you will need a carnet de passages, and rules about large motorcycles and travel permits change, so check current regulations and travel advice before you go. The rewards, for those who make it, are extraordinary.
t.alamut castle and related fortifications:
The rock of Alamut rises out of the valley like the prow of a ship, and it is easy to see why Hassan-i Sabbah chose it. In 1090 this Ismaili missionary took the castle, reportedly without bloodshed, and made it the headquarters of a movement that would defy empires for over a century and a half. From Alamut he directed a network of fortresses across Persia and Syria, and from here grew the legend of the Assassins, the name that European travellers like Marco Polo attached to the Nizaris, with tales of a hidden paradise garden and young men drugged with hashish. Most historians treat those stories as myth, but they made Alamut famous.

Hassan was a scholar as well as a political leader, and Alamut was renowned for its library. In 1256 the Mongol armies of Hulagu Khan arrived, and the last Nizari ruler surrendered the castle. The Persian historian Juvayni, who accompanied the Mongols, was allowed to inspect the library and saved some works before the rest was destroyed. The fortress was dismantled, though it was later used as a prison.

Today the ruins sit on the summit of the rock above the village of Gazor Khan. A steep stairway leads up from the village, and at the top you can see the remains of walls, cisterns and rooms carved into the stone. Excavation and restoration work has been ongoing, and parts may be covered with scaffolding. The views from the top over the valley, the river and the snow-capped peaks of the Alborz are magnificent.

The valley itself is lovely, with orchards, rice fields and villages, and the Alamut river winding through. It is a cooler, greener world than the dusty plain around Qazvin. The road over the mountains from Qazvin is a highlight of any ride in northern Iran, climbing in a long series of hairpins to a high pass before dropping into the valley. Surfaces are mixed, and weather can change quickly, with snow on the pass from late autumn to spring.

Qazvin, a couple of hours away, has fuel, hotels and restaurants. Gazor Khan has guesthouses and small cafés serving tea and simple meals. Riding in Iran requires a carnet de passages and careful planning, so check current rules, permits and travel advice before setting off.
t.sirkuh fortification@36.4,50.4:
North of Qazvin, the Alborz rises in folded, ochre and green ridges, and somewhere in those ridges lies Širkūh, one of the mountain strongholds of the Nizari Ismailis, the sect that held the valleys of Alamut and Rudbar from the late eleventh century until the Mongols came. Their founder in Persia, Hasan-i Sabbah, took the castle of Alamut in 1090, and from it a network of fortresses grew up across these mountains. The rides that pass here link several of them, Qosṭinlār and Navizaršāh among them.

What survives at places like Širkūh is usually fragmentary: rock-cut cisterns, stubs of wall, terraces on an outcrop that commands a valley. Do not expect a restored castle. What you get instead is the logic of the place, a summit with water, food stores and a view of every approach, which allowed small garrisons to hold out against much larger armies. In 1256 Hulagu's Mongols forced the surrender of the Ismaili leader and demolished the castles one by one, and the legends of the so-called Assassins, much embroidered by European writers, did the rest.

The road from Qazvin north into the Alamut valley is one of the great rides of northern Iran. It climbs over a high pass with long views back across the plain, then drops into a steep valley of orchards, rice terraces and small villages, with the Alamut river cutting through. The tarmac is generally decent but narrow, with tight hairpins, rockfall after rain and the occasional livestock crossing. Snow can close the high section in winter, and spring brings meltwater and landslides. Late spring and autumn are ideal, with clear air and poplars turning gold.

There is no town of any size close to Širkūh itself, so treat Qazvin, Ābyek or Alvand, all around forty kilometres away, as your real supply points. Fill the tank and carry water before you head into the mountains. Qazvin itself is worth a night: a former Safavid capital with a fine old bazaar, mosques and caravanserais, and a lively food scene with local sweets and rice dishes.

As in the rest of Iran, foreign riders need a carnet, a valid visa and an up to date read on local rules. Village hospitality in the Alamut area is generous, and a stop for tea in a roadside teahouse with a view of the valley tends to stretch longer than you planned.
t.chahar bagh@36.3,51.2:
There is more than one Chahar-Bagh in Iran, because the name simply means four gardens and describes the classical garden layout, but the coordinates here put it in the Alborz range north-west of Karaj, in the mountain country between Tehran's plain and the Caspian. This is the playground of the capital. On Fridays, when the Iranian weekend begins, the roads fill with families heading up to cool valleys, streams and picnic spots under the walnut trees.

The Alborz are young, steep mountains, the highest of them capped by Damavand, a volcanic cone that on clear days stands white above everything. Here the valleys are narrower and greener than anything on the dry plateau to the south, with orchards in the bottoms, shepherds' huts on the slopes and old stone villages built for protection. A fortification in the name of the site, Qosṭinlār, points to how long people have been guarding passes in this region, because routes across the range were always strategic, whether for armies, merchants or pilgrims. I can't tell you more about the exact ruin, and it is wiser to ask locally than to trust a guess.

For riding, the main mountain roads through this area are among the best in Iran: long climbs, hairpins, tunnels and big drops, with a lot of truck and weekend traffic on the busiest routes. Go midweek if you can, start early and expect cold at the top even in summer, because passes in the Alborz sit well above two thousand metres and weather turns fast, with fog, rain and occasional snow outside the warm months. Surfaces vary, so watch for potholes and gravel on the corners after a thaw or a storm.

Karaj, a big city, is the sensible place to fill up, and small villages along the way will have little more than a shop or a tea house. Carry water, keep fuel above half and plan lunch in a village, because a plate of grilled fish or kebab and a pot of tea are the standard mountain refuel.

The best months are May, June and September to early October, when snow has gone from the lower slopes and the days are warm. Winter means closures and ice on high stretches, so check the road before committing.
t.segment pampa del inca finca de chanaral:
The Atacama desert is the driest place on earth outside the poles, and the Inca crossed it on foot. The Qhapaq Ñan, the great Inca road system, included a southern branch that ran from Cusco down into what is now northern Chile, and this segment between Pampa del Inca and the farm of Chañaral lies in the region of Atacama, close to the town of Diego de Almagro. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Qhapaq Ñan in 2014. The road here is little more than a cleared track marked with stone lines and small cairns, running across gravel plains and dry watercourses, and I cannot describe the exact spot, but the setting is clear: pale hills, blue sky and a silence that you can almost hear.

The name Diego de Almagro belongs to the Spanish conquistador who came this way in 1536, leading an expedition from Peru across the Andes in search of a second Inca treasure, and who suffered terribly in the cold. The town of Diego de Almagro, with about eighteen thousand people, grew around the copper and railway industry, and has fuel, shops and food. It is the sensible last stop for services before heading into the high desert.

For motorcyclists the area is a dream. The road east from the coast climbs to the Paso San Francisco, over four thousand seven hundred metres, on the border with Argentina, passing salt flats, lagoons with flamingos and the huge cone of the Ojos del Salado, the highest active volcano in the world, at nearly seven thousand metres. The road is paved in parts and gravel in others, with strong wind, thin air and almost no traffic. Fuel is limited and distances are vast, so carry spare and water, and tell someone your plan.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with clear skies, and winter nights are very cold. The desert flowers after rare rains, and when it happens, the plains turn pink and purple for a few weeks, an event worth waiting for. Mind the sun and the altitude.
t.yengeh emam@35.9,50.7:
The Trans-Iranian Railway is one of the great engineering projects of the twentieth century. Built in the 1930s on the orders of Reza Shah, it links the Caspian Sea in the north with the Persian Gulf in the south, a distance of about 1,400 kilometres, across mountain ranges, deserts and gorges. The route climbs through hundreds of bridges and tunnels, often using spiral tunnels to gain height, and it was built by engineers from many countries, including Germans, Austrians and Danes. UNESCO listed it in 2021, and Yengeh Emām, in the plain west of Tehran, lies on its line. I cannot tell you what the station looks like today, but the line itself is the story.

The surrounding country is the fertile plain of Alborz province, between Karaj, a sprawling city of well over a million people, and the town of Nazarabad, with more than two hundred thousand. Orchards, poplar lines and market gardens lie among the new suburbs, and the Alborz mountains rise to the north, their upper slopes white with snow until late spring. In the old days this was farmland supplying Tehran, and traces of the older landscape survive in the villages.

For riders, Karaj is the gateway to one of Iran's classic motorbike roads. The Chalus road, which climbs from Karaj over the high Alborz and drops to the Caspian coast, runs along a deep valley and past a large reservoir, then through tunnels and a mountain pass at more than two thousand metres, before plunging into the green forest of the north. The scenery changes in a few hours from dry gravel to dripping woodland. The road is busy at weekends, when half of Tehran heads for the sea, and surfaces vary. Go on a weekday if you can, and expect fog on the northern side.

Nazarabad, ten kilometres away, has plenty of fuel and food, and Karaj has all the services of a large city. The traffic in the plain is heavy and fast, so ride with care. Travel conditions for foreign visitors are changeable, so check before you plan anything. If you are able to go, a tea and a pastry at a station cafe, with the line running behind, is a good way to end the day.
t.khoshk e daran@36.7,51.1:
Between the Caspian shore and the first folds of the Alborz mountains, western Mazandaran packs more variety into thirty kilometres than most regions manage in three hundred. Khoshk-e-Daran lies in that squeeze, a few kilometres from Nashtarud and a short run from Tonekabon, which is the proper town of the area, with Chalus further east. The sea is close enough to smell, yet the hills behind are steep, and everything between is orange groves, rice paddies, tea bushes and tidy villages with steep tin roofs designed for rain.

That rain is the first fact about riding here. The Caspian coast of Iran is damp, often grey, and humid enough in summer to make the afternoon sticky, so the trip is nicest in late spring and early autumn, when the air is clearer and the forest is at its brightest. The coastal road is busy with local traffic and trucks, and it has the slightly ragged rhythm of any holiday coast, with fruit stalls, roadside kebab stands and sudden junctions. The real pleasure is turning inland. The side valleys climb quickly into the Hyrcanian forest, the ancient broadleaf woodland of beech, hornbeam and oak that survived the ice ages along this coast and that now carries World Heritage status. Roads there narrow, switchback, and sometimes wear a coat of damp leaves, so ride them slowly and expect wet patches even on dry days.

Culture here is quite distinct from the Iranian plateau. People speak Mazandarani and Gilaki alongside Persian, cook with walnuts, pomegranate paste and fresh herbs, and build houses on stilts or with wide wooden verandas against the damp. Rice is the staple, and fish from the Caspian, including sturgeon in the past, has long been part of local life. Ask for a cup of tea in a village and you will probably be brought one, very hot and very sweet.

Nashtarud is a small town of a bit under six thousand, so you will find fuel and basic supplies there, and Tonekabon offers a wider choice. Beyond that the mountains thin out services quickly. I do not know of a single named monument at this precise spot, so use it as a base for the forest roads and the fortified hill sites that the ride names, and keep a rain layer packed.
t.kojoor@36.5,51.7:
Kojoor is a green name on a green map. It lies in the forested hills of Mazandaran province, above the Caspian coast between Nowshahr and Chalus, in a region that Iranians simply call the north, as if every other part of the country were an afterthought. The coast road below is a string of resort towns, tea and citrus gardens, and the traffic that comes with them. Up here the pace slows considerably.

The valley of the Kojoor river cuts back into the Alborz, and the road follows it into oak and beech forest that grows thick enough to turn the light a deep underwater green. These are the Hyrcanian forests, relics of a woodland that once ran unbroken around the southern Caspian and that has stayed damp and shady since before the last ice age. Mist forms in the mornings, moss grows on every north-facing trunk, and after rain the smell of wet earth and leaf mould is powerful. Wildlife is shy but real, with wild boar, jackals, and roe deer in the woods, and if you are very lucky and very quiet the odd trace of larger animals higher up.

For riding, this is slower, narrower, tighter country than the plateaus of central Iran. Bends come close together, sometimes with gravel or mud washed across them, and in the villages you share the tarmac with tractors, walkers and the occasional cow. That is a recipe for a gentle pace and a lot of attention to the surface. The best time is late spring or early autumn, and a dry day after wet ones, when the forest glows. Summer is humid and busy with holidaymakers escaping Tehran, while winter can bring fog and ice on higher stretches.

A famous road connects this coast to Tehran over the mountains, the Chalus road, which climbs through spectacular, crowded and dramatic terrain to a tunnel on the ridge. It is tempting, but on weekends it clogs with Tehran families in cars, so go midweek if you can.

Nowshahr, about nineteen kilometres away, and Chalus, a little further, are the places for fuel, food and a bed. Small village shops sell bread, cheese and fruit, and a glass of tea is rarely refused. I know the region better than the village itself, so take the general picture as the guide rather than any specific stop.
t.segment rio de la sal pampa del inca@-26:
Out here the Atacama stops being a postcard and becomes a working landscape: pale gravel plains, dry washes, and a horizon that stays the same colour for an hour at a time. The Río de la Sal gets its name honestly. Whatever water the Andes send down this way picks up minerals on the trip, and what survives to the surface leaves white crusts along the banks. Pampa del Inca, the broad flat beside it, is the kind of name you only get where travellers have been crossing the same ground for centuries.

That is the point of the place. This is a piece of the Qhapaq Ñan, the Inca road system that ran from the highlands of Cusco down the spine of the continent, and the stretch through the Atacama region is one of the Chilean sections recognised as part of the World Heritage listing. The Inca did not build here to admire the view. They needed a dependable line across a desert where the next water could be two days away, so the track follows what little there is: dry valleys, the odd spring, flat ground for walkers and llama trains.

For a rider the reward is scale and silence, so plan around the lack of everything else. The nearest proper town is Diego de Almagro, about 37 km away, with some 18,000 people, so that is where you top up the tank and buy water and food before heading in. Do not count on anything out here. Carry more fuel than the map says you need, a litre or two of water beyond your own thirst, and a phone with the route saved offline, because signal is a rumour. Gravel and sand can show up without warning on tracks like this, so ride it as an adventure road, not a motorway.

Mornings and late afternoons are the best hours. Midday light flattens everything into glare, while low sun pulls out the ridges and the colour in the rock, and the air smells of dust and warm stone. The wind picks up in the afternoon and carries grit, so keep your visor clean. The altitude here is considerable even though the ground looks flat, and the nights turn cold quickly. A spare layer is cheap insurance.

The town you pass through on the way takes its name from Diego de Almagro, the Spanish conquistador who led an expedition south from Peru into Chile in the 1530s and came through this same high, dry country. His men suffered badly in the crossing, and many say that experience helped sour the first Spanish impression of Chile. Standing on the pampa, it is not hard to see why.

Think of this as the same journey seen from the other end of the segment. The label here is Portal del Inca to Río de la Sal, and the first half of that name is the interesting one. Portal suggests a gateway, a place where the trail passes through a narrowing or a pass and the ground begins to change. Without a signed monument underfoot, the useful thing to say is what the surrounding country does: the Atacama's interior basins rise gradually toward the Andean crest, and the Inca engineers used each step in that rise as a staging post.

Rivers in this part of Chile are rarely rivers in the European sense. The Río de la Sal is a thin ribbon that dries and floods with the season, and the vegetation hugs it tightly: a green seam, some grasses, and then a sudden edge where the desert resumes. Animals know that seam well. You may see vicuña or guanaco on the slopes above, usually lifting their heads together and then deciding you are not worth the effort. Flamingos turn up at the salt lakes higher in this part of the Andes, though not necessarily here.

There is no town on the doorstep. The nearest settlements of any size lie a long way off along the main road, and for supplies you should think of Diego de Almagro, with its fuel, shops and a bed, as your base. Filling up to the brim there and carrying extra is not caution for its own sake; it is simply how the region works. Help, if you need it, is slow to arrive, so tell someone where you are going and treat every unmarked fork as a decision.

The surface is the main thing to understand. Tracks like these are graded in some places and washboarded or sandy in others, and after rare rain a dry wash can turn soft in minutes. Keep your speed honest, look far ahead for the darker patches that mean sand, and give yourself margin on gradients where gravel sits loose. In return you get a line of sight that reaches for dozens of kilometres, a sky that goes properly dark at night, and the odd sense that you are following people who walked here five hundred years ago with far less than a fuel tank to worry about.
t.ilan fortification@36.4,50.7:
The coordinates fall in the Alborz mountains of northern Iran, in the high country around the Alamut valley where Qazvin province meets the Caspian slopes, and I will say plainly that I cannot tell you what this particular fortification looked like on the day you stand at it. What I can say is that this is castle country on a grand scale. The Alborz are a wall of steep, folded mountains that rise above the Caspian coast to the peak of Damavand and beyond, and every ridge worth defending seems to have a ruin on it, mud-brick and stone ramparts clinging to the crags.

The most famous is Alamut itself, the stronghold of Hassan-i Sabbah and the Nizari Ismailis, whom crusader writers called the Assassins. They held a string of mountain castles from the late eleventh century until the Mongols destroyed them in 1256. The story of their young recruits and the garden of paradise is mostly legend, but the real castles are dramatic enough, perched on rock spurs with a single path up and a single cistern cut into stone. Smaller forts like this one belong to the same landscape of passes, valleys and small walled villages.

The riding here is serious and beautiful. Roads climb from the plain at Qazvin through foothills of orchards and walnut trees, then wind in tight bends along river gorges, with sheer rock on one side and a drop on the other. The Chalus road, over the high passes to the Caspian, is among the great mountain roads of the region, but it is also heavily used by lorries and holiday traffic, and snow closes the upper sections for months in winter. Surfaces can be broken, landslides leave gravel on the road after rain, and mist comes down fast.

Villages in the valleys have little more than a shop and a tea house, so fill the tank in Qazvin or Rudbar before heading up. Come between May and October, when the passes are open and the walnut orchards are green, and carry a layer for the altitude. Check current travel advice and local road conditions, and leave plenty of daylight for the return.
t.the persian caravanserai@35.1,51.4:
A day's journey for a loaded camel was about thirty or forty kilometres, and every caravan road in Persia was punctuated at that interval by a building where men and animals could rest. The caravanserai was a walled courtyard with a single gate, rooms around the inside for travellers, stables and stores for the animals, and a well or a cistern in the middle. The Persian caravanserais, a group of fifty-four of which UNESCO listed in 2023, are the survivors of a network that carried silk, spices, cloth and ideas across the region for centuries. Many were built or repaired under Shah Abbas I in the early seventeenth century, who wanted trade to pass through his territory and to be safe.

The country south-west of Tehran, near Eqbalieh and Varamin, lies along the old road to Qom and the south, across a flat plain of salt and dust. The buildings that survive are mostly of mud brick, with arched passages and a plain, robust character that has withstood centuries of heat and wind. It is a place to imagine a very different kind of traffic, of camels, merchants and pilgrims arriving at dusk, and where the sound of bells and the smell of dung and smoke filled the courtyard.

Here too runs the Trans-Iranian Railway, built between 1927 and 1938, which crosses the mountains and the desert from the Caspian to the Gulf and is itself on the World Heritage List. The old caravan road and the new railway tell the same story of a country that has always depended on moving goods across difficult ground.

For a rider the plain is fast, flat and exposed, with big trucks and long straight roads. Heat in summer is intense, and dust storms can reduce visibility. Varamin, with a hundred and eighty thousand people, and the small city of Eqbalieh have fuel and food, and the Friday mosque in Varamin is a fine Mongol-period building from the early fourteenth century. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for the ride.

Take water, and stay on the paved roads. Rules for foreign motorcyclists in Iran are strict and change, so check before you plan a trip.
t.cachi@-25.1,-66.2:
Cachí sits at around 2,300 metres in the Calchaquí valleys of Salta province, and everything about it seems to have been made quiet by altitude and dryness. White adobe houses line narrow streets, the plaza is shaded by trees, and the church has a roof and doors made from the wood of the cardón, a tall columnar cactus that grows on the slopes around. The backdrop is the Nevado de Cachi, a snow-capped peak in the range that stands above 6,000 metres.

This is wine and pepper country, and the sun here is fierce. The old Calchaquí people lived here long before the Incas and then the Spanish arrived, and their descendants still keep alive weaving, pottery and a fondness for corn dishes like humita and locro. The archaeological museum in town shows pieces from the pre-Hispanic past, and a few hundred metres off the plaza the pace of life seems closer to the nineteenth century than the twenty-first.

The riding is the main reason many people pass through. Ruta 40 here is a famous motorcycle road. From the north, riders climb the Cuesta del Obispo, a gravel and then paved ascent with sharp bends, through Los Cardones National Park, where thousands of cardón cacti stand like sentries on the Recta del Tin Tin, a long straight line across the plain. South of Cachí the road follows the valley toward Molinos and Cafayate, with colourful rock formations and vineyards. Wind and altitude are factors, and nights are cold even in summer. Mornings are clearest.

Cachí is a small town but has the necessary basics, with a fuel pump and simple restaurants and guesthouses, though supplies can run low, so it is wise to top up before and after. Try empanadas salteñas with a glass of local Torrontés. At this height you may find yourself breathing harder than usual, so take it easy on the first day.
t.cafayate@-26.1,-66.0:
Cafayate is a wine town at about sixteen hundred metres in the Calchaquí valleys of Salta province, in the dry north-west of Argentina, and it is the reward at the end of a long ride south. After days of high desert, salt flats and unpaved passes, you come down into a flat valley full of vines and suddenly there is shade, cold white wine and a plaza where people sit for hours. The mountains stand on both sides, brown and bare, and the light is so clear that distances seem shorter than they are.

The valley's signature grape is Torrontés, a white variety that thrives in the thin air and strong sun and produces a wine that smells of roses and peach. The vineyards here are among the highest in the world, and several bodegas on the edge of town offer tastings, with long afternoon lunches that pair the wine with grilled meat, goat cheese and empanadas salteñas, the small spicy ones with a juicy filling. If you plan to ride afterwards, be sensible with the tasting spoons.

The roads around Cafayate are some of the best in the north-west. To the north, Ruta 40 climbs through the valley toward Angastaco and Molinos, partly unpaved and often covered with loose gravel. To the south and east, the road through the Quebrada de las Conchas, a gorge of red, orange and ochre sandstone, offers wonderful riding with sweeping views, rock formations known as the Devil's Throat and the Amphitheatre, and light that changes by the hour. The wind picks up in the afternoon, sometimes with serious force, so start early and keep a tight grip. Summer thunderstorms can flood the gorge floor, and dust in the dry season lingers behind every vehicle.

Cafayate has about twelve thousand people and has everything a rider needs: petrol stations, workshops of a modest kind, hostels, restaurants and a good bakery. The nights are cool, even in summer, and in winter the temperature can fall below freezing, so pack a warm layer. April and May, after the harvest, are lovely, with golden vine leaves, while the winter months are dry and clear. Sit in the plaza, buy an ice cream and let the long ride settle.
t.segment rio de la sal pampa del inca@-26:
Here the Atacama is not a single desert but a collection of them, and the stretch around Río de la Sal sits in its high, empty heart. The land is a pale expanse of volcanic rock and sand, with salt-crusted basins, dry riverbeds and enormous distances. Nothing grows here without help. The sky is absurdly blue, the air is thin, and at night the stars come out in a density most people have never seen.

The Incas knew this route. Their road, part of the Qhapaq Ñan network that UNESCO listed in 2014, ran south from the Andean highlands through the desert toward the fertile valleys of central Chile, with waystations placed a day's walk apart. A later traveller of a very different kind was the Spanish conquistador Diego de Almagro, who crossed the Andes in 1536 on his way to Chile through a high pass in winter and lost a large part of his party to cold and hunger. The nearest town, Diego de Almagro, carries his name, a slightly ironic honour given what the journey cost.

A rider here is in remote country. Main roads are paved but long and empty, with strong winds sweeping across the plain, and side tracks are sand, gravel and washboard. Altitude is considerable, and mornings are cold even in summer. Mining trucks run on some of these roads, and drivers are used to having them to themselves. Vicuñas and guanacos graze on sparse grass in damp hollows, and you may see a fox at dusk. The geology is a show in itself, with colour bands in the rock walls and old lava flows frozen mid-pour.

The practical rule is simple: fill up in town. Diego de Almagro, about thirty-three kilometres away and home to eighteen thousand people, is the nearest place with fuel and shops, and beyond it services thin out fast. Carry more water than seems reasonable, extra fuel if the bike's range is short, and a phone with offline maps, since coverage disappears. Spring and autumn are best, while the winter months can bring snow at altitude and summer brings afternoon heat in the lowlands.
t.segment portal del inca rio de la sal@-2:
The name Portal del Inca suggests a gate, and in a way it is one: a threshold on the road that the Incas drove south across the desert from the Andean heartland. Qhapaq Ñan is the name of the whole system, a network of tracks that stretched for thousands of kilometres and carried armies, tax goods and runners with messages. In the Atacama it was built simply, since the ground was hard and dry. Stones were cleared and lined up to mark the path, and the tambos, or roadside stations, stood at intervals with stores of food and water for officials.

Because this is a segment rather than a single monument, you will not find a ticket office or a signboard that explains everything. What you see is a dry high plain of pale volcanic soil and rock, with distant cones of dormant volcanoes and the odd salt flat shining like spilled paint. Silence is part of the place, broken only by wind, and in the early morning the air is crisp enough to see your breath even in the warm months. The riding is open and exposed. Tracks branch off the main routes, some firm and some sandy, and mining trucks run on the better ones.

The wind is the main hazard. It can come up fast in the afternoon and push a bike sideways across a gravel road, so travel in the early hours when the air is still. Altitude saps the engine and the rider, so take it easy and drink water often. There is no mobile signal in many places, and a breakdown can mean a long wait, which makes it wise to ride with a companion or to tell someone your plan. Night temperatures drop sharply, even in summer, and frost is common in winter.

No services exist out here, and the pin has no nearby town in the data, so plan everything from the larger places. Fill the tank completely in Diego de Almagro or in Copiapó before you leave the paved road, and carry enough water and food for a full day beyond what you think you need. Late spring and autumn give the best conditions. In these months the light is soft, the days are warm, and the old road feels less like an ordeal and more like a long, strange privilege.
t.rotorua lakes and forest@-36.2,174.6:
This point lies at the northern edge of the Auckland region, near the Northland boundary, in the country between Wellsford and the coast at Te Arai and Mangawhai. It is farmland with a sea at its edge: rolling green hills, dairy and sheep farms, patches of native bush, and then the long, empty surf beaches of the east coast, where the sand is pale and the water cold. Wellsford, fourteen kilometres away, is a small service town on State Highway 1, and Warkworth, twenty-two kilometres to the south, is the bigger one.

State Highway 1 is the main road north out of Auckland, and this section carries a lot of traffic, trucks and holiday cars, particularly on Friday afternoons. The better ride is off it. Roads lead east to the Pakiri coast, through gentle farmland with long views, and to the little settlements of Mangawhai Heads and Te Arai, where you find a harbour, a cliff walk and surf beaches. The road surface is sealed but often narrow, with sharp little corners, gravel patches at junctions and farm vehicles, so keep an eye ahead. North of here, the Brynderwyn Hills section of the highway has long been prone to slips in wet weather, and delays are common, so check the conditions. Wind and sudden rain are normal, even in summer.

A little north, Waipu is a surprising place. It was settled in the 1850s by Scottish Highlanders who had first emigrated to Nova Scotia, and then, led by a preacher, moved on by ship to New Zealand. The town still holds a Highland gathering every New Year's Day, with caber tossing and pipe bands, and a small museum tells their story. Wellsford itself has a few cafes and bakeries, pies and fish and chips, and fuel stations on the highway, so it is a convenient place for a quick refuel and a bite.

Plan your food and fuel in Wellsford or Warkworth, because the coastal roads have little. The Mahurangi and Matakana areas, close by, have wineries, farmers' markets and lively cafes, while the inland roads offer quiet, curving riding across the farms. In autumn, the light is clear and soft, and the evenings are mild.
t.waitakere ranges and piha@-36.8,174.2:
This coordinate falls out in the Tasman Sea, west of Muriwai, so the honest way to describe the spot is by the coast it looks toward. Here the west coast of Auckland runs north from the Waitākere Ranges in a long, dark line of black iron-sand beach, backed by dunes and pine forest, and the surf comes in heavy from thousands of kilometres of open ocean. Muriwai Beach, nearly twenty kilometres away, is the nearest settlement, and it has the gannet colony on its northern headland, where Australasian gannets nest on the cliff tops from about August to March, a noisy and pungent spectacle, with a viewing platform reached by a short, steep path.

South of Muriwai, the Waitākere Ranges rise in a block of rugged, rainforest-covered hills, a regional park of more than sixteen thousand hectares that was once heavily logged for kauri timber. The great trees were cut and dragged to the coast, and the old dams and tramways are part of the landscape now. Today the park protects forests of kauri, tree ferns and rimu, with waterfalls and steep valleys, though the kauri dieback disease has forced the closure of many tracks, and signs ask you to stay out of closed areas and clean your boots at the stations. At the foot of the ranges, Piha is the best-known surf beach, with the great volcanic dome of Lion Rock standing at one end. It is a place of rips and strong currents, so swim only between the flags where lifeguards patrol.

For a rider, the roads of the ranges are a delight. The Scenic Drive and the road to Piha twist through the forest in tight bends, climbing and dropping, with moss-covered banks and tree ferns overhanging the road. The surface is variable, often damp and slippery, with leaf litter and gravel on the corners, and the road is narrow, so go gently, particularly on blind bends. Traffic is heavy at weekends, with day-trippers, but weekday mornings are calm.

Services are thin out here. The village of Muriwai has a store, and Parakai, twenty-five kilometres away, has fuel and more shops, and the hot pools are good after a damp day. The city lies a half hour away, so fill up before you go. Take a warm layer, as the west coast is much cooler and windier than the city.
t.east cape long adventure photo pull off@:
The point on the map sits on the Hauraki Gulf coast just east of Warkworth, in the country around the Mahurangi Peninsula and Kawau Bay, and it is some of the gentlest and most appealing coastal land within reach of Auckland. Here the shore is a tangle of sheltered inlets, mangrove creeks, oyster beds and small white beaches, with islands scattered across the gulf. The hills are green and rolling, grazed by sheep and cattle, with pockets of native bush and the occasional vineyard.

Warkworth, the main town, sits on the Mahurangi River, and was once a busy shipping port for timber and farm produce, with a few old colonial buildings still standing. Further along the coast, Kawau Island, just offshore, was the home of Sir George Grey, the colonial governor, who bought it in the 1860s, filled it with exotic animals and built a mansion, now a museum reached by ferry. Wallabies, introduced by Grey, still survive on the island. On the mainland, Tawharanui Regional Park, a predator-free sanctuary, has been restored with the help of volunteers, and birds such as kiwi, takahē and brown teal have been released there, which gives the bush a bright chorus in the morning.

Matakana, a few minutes inland, is a village with a lively Saturday farmers' market, wineries, a cinema and craft breweries, and it fills with visitors from the city at weekends, so the roads are busier then. The riding itself is relaxed: winding country roads with good surface, well-banked curves and glimpses of the water. Some sections are narrow and shaded, with patches of gravel, and farm gates and stock trucks are a hazard. The best months are late spring and autumn, when the days are warm and the roads are dry, and winter rain can make the roads slippery.

Warkworth is twenty kilometres away and has fuel, supermarkets and a good run of cafes and bakeries, so it is the place to fill up before heading out. The nearest larger town is on the northern edge of Auckland. For a meal, the fish and chips and fresh oysters of the gulf are hard to beat, and the sunsets across the water can be stunning, so take your time and enjoy the light.
t.deyr e gachin@35.1,51.4:
Deyr-e Gachin is a caravanserai on the edge of the desert south-east of Tehran, a fortified rest house of mud brick and stone, built to shelter merchants and their animals on a long road across the dry plain. Such buildings were the motels of old Persia, set a day's march apart along the trade routes, with a gate wide enough for loaded camels, a courtyard for the animals and rooms for the travellers around it. This one stands in a wide flat landscape of salt flats, gravel and low hills, and the light is bright and hard.

I do not know the full history of this building, and it is better to say so than to guess at dates. What is clear is that it belongs to a long tradition of roads and trade, which linked the cities of the Iranian plateau with the markets of Mesopotamia, India and Central Asia. The Silk Road was not one road, but many, and caravanserais like this one were the places where goods and news changed hands.

The nearest town is Eqbalieh, about twenty-nine kilometres away, with some 37,000 people, and it has fuel and shops. The road there crosses a dry, open plain, with the great salt desert, the Dasht-e Kavir, not far to the east, and wind can raise dust. Fuel stations are fewer than in the settled north, so keep the tank full. The ride continues to Tehran, where the Golestan Palace, a jewel of tilework and mirrors from the Qajar period, is a UNESCO World Heritage site and a world away from this silent stone yard.

Spring and autumn are the best times, when the days are warm and the nights cool. Summer heat is fierce, and shade is scarce. Bring plenty of water, and wear a scarf against dust. Standing in the old courtyard at dusk, with the walls glowing and the desert silent, it is easy to imagine the camel bells and the smoke of cooking fires.
t.new plymouth@-39.1,174.1:
Mount Taranaki rises from the flat dairy country of the west coast of New Zealand's North Island like a drawing of a volcano, a nearly perfect cone, 2,518 metres high, often wrapped in cloud and capped with snow. It is also known as Egmont, a name given by Captain Cook, though the Māori name is the older and more widely used. New Plymouth, the city on the coast at its northern flank, sits in the mountain's shadow, with the Tasman Sea on the other side, and the two dominate every view.

The city has about fifty thousand people and a more relaxed air than Auckland. Pukekura Park, a green valley of lakes, ferns and fountains, runs through the middle of town. On the seafront, a coastal walkway leads to the Wind Wand, a tall, slender kinetic sculpture by Len Lye that sways in the breeze, and to the Te Rewa Rewa Bridge, a white arch shaped like a whale's backbone, framing Taranaki behind it. The area's history includes the land wars of the 1860s, whose scars are still part of the region's story, and the more recent gas fields offshore.

Riders have a choice of roads. Surf Highway 45 circles the mountain's southern coast through dairy farms and small beach towns, with views of black sand beaches, surf breaks and the sea. Inland, the Forgotten World Highway leaves from Stratford on the eastern side, a long and winding road through hills and old farm country, with a tunnel carved by hand and a strange republic of its own. Roads up the mountain itself, such as Egmont Road, climb through forest to the national park with views over the plain. Weather can change in minutes, with cloud closing the mountain and rain sweeping in.

New Plymouth has fuel, food and rooms in plenty, and Waitara to the north adds more. Fill up before the Forgotten World Highway, where services are scarce. Summer is the best season, though showers can come any time.
t.east cape@-37.0,174.5:
Where Auckland ends, New Zealand begins, and this is the place to see it. The coordinates fall on the rugged west side of the Waitākere Ranges, near the mouth of the Manukau Harbour at Whatipu, a wild corner of black sand, dunes, caves and sea cliffs, reached by narrow roads that wind down from the hills. It is a far cry from the East Cape, whose long journey the label describes, and is a fine place to finish a day.

Whatipu is a dramatic place. The Manukau Harbour has one of the most dangerous bar crossings in the world, and in the nineteenth century many ships were wrecked here, including the HMS Orpheus in 1863, New Zealand's worst maritime disaster, in which nearly two hundred sailors died. Wide dunes and a long beach face the Tasman Sea, and a sea cave, once used for dances, opens at the foot of the cliffs. Sea birds gather on the rocks, and gannets from the colony at Muriwai, up the coast, patrol the waves.

The road in is the attraction. Huia Road, from Titirangi, twists and turns through thick native forest, past stands of kauri, with a mix of blind corners, gravel patches and sudden views over the harbour. Karekare, another black sand beach nearby, was the setting for scenes in the film The Piano. The surface is narrow, often damp and shaded, and slips and tree falls can block sections after storms, so check conditions and slow down. In summer, beaches fill with surfers and walkers at weekends.

Titirangi, the village on the edge of the ranges, has cafes, galleries and fuel, and is the last real service before the coast. Take plenty of fuel and water, since there are no shops at Whatipu. Mist and rain sweep in off the Tasman quickly, and temperatures can drop. The colours at sunset, when the sky glows over the dunes, are a good reward.
t.wadi darbat@17.1,54.4:
Wadi Darbat lies in the hills behind Salalah, in Dhofar, the southern province of Oman, and it is one of those places that does not seem to belong to Arabia. For three months in summer, from roughly late June to September, the khareef, the south-west monsoon, wraps the coastal mountains in mist and drizzle, and the slopes turn from brown to green. The wadi fills with water, a lake forms, a waterfall tumbles over a limestone cliff, and the grass is thick enough for cattle and camels to graze in the cool damp.

The khareef is the great event of the Omani year, and visitors from across the Gulf drive here to enjoy the weather, so during the season the road to Darbat is busy with cars, picnickers and the occasional camel on the tarmac. The rest of the year the place is quieter, drier and hotter, and the waterfall may shrink to a trickle or vanish. The limestone terrain also holds sinkholes, caves and travertine pools. If you ride here outside the monsoon, you will see a different, starker country.

The roads from Salalah, about thirty-eight kilometres to the south-west, are good and well maintained, and climb through the hills in broad curves. In the khareef, fog can reduce visibility to a few metres, and the tarmac is slippery, so slow down and use your lights. Camels wander across the road with total confidence, and a collision would be a disaster for both of you, so give them time. The best months for riding are October to March, when the air is clear and warm, and the temperatures are comfortable.

Salalah has everything you need in the way of fuel, food and hotels, and there are small cafes and fruit stalls near the wadi in season. Dhofar is also the home of frankincense, the resin of the Boswellia tree, which grows in the dry hills behind the coast and has been traded for thousands of years. Take a moment to smell the burning resin in a market, and you will understand why it was worth more than gold.
t.jebel samhan@17.1,54.7:
Jebel Samhan is the highest part of the mountain wall that rises behind the Dhofar coast, east of Salalah, and it is one of the wildest corners of Oman. The plateau, a rolling limestone upland of about eighteen hundred metres in places, is cut by deep wadis and cliffs that fall steeply toward the Arabian Sea, and much of it is protected as a nature reserve, home to the Arabian leopard, one of the rarest big cats in the world. You are very unlikely to see one, since they are shy and few, but the idea that they are up there adds to the mood.

The area is also known for its sinkholes, one of which, Tawi Attair, is among the deepest in the world, and for its frankincense trees and ancient tombs. In the summer monsoon, the khareef, the plateau is wrapped in thick mist and the air turns cool and damp. In winter, it is clear, dry and often windy, with long views toward the sea.

The road here climbs from the coast on steep switchbacks, and the surface and the width vary, so take it slowly and check conditions locally. The gradients are steep and the bends tight, and there are long drops at the edge of the road, so a loaded bike needs to be well handled. Camels and goats wander onto the tarmac. In the khareef the road may be wet and foggy, and in the heat of summer the engine can suffer on the long climb.

There are no services up here, and the nearest fuel is on the coast, at Mirbat or Taqah, or in Salalah, so fill the tank before the climb. Water and food should be carried, since the plateau is empty and the sun is strong. Shade is scarce, and the sky is huge. The birdlife includes vultures and eagles that ride the thermals above the cliffs. The wind, which blows nearly all the time, brings a smell of dry herbs and stone. Take a moment to look down over the edge at the sea and the green coastal plain far below.
t.mirbat@17.0,54.7:
Mirbat is a small, quiet town on the Arabian Sea, about seventy kilometres east of Salalah, and it has more history than its size suggests. For centuries it was a trading port, exporting frankincense and fine horses to India, and a few old houses with carved doors and wooden shutters survive in the old quarter, though many are in ruins. The town has a low white fort, a pretty beach and a fishing harbour where the boats come in at dawn, and the calm of the place is a relief after the traffic of Salalah.

It also has a place in more recent history. In July 1972, during the Dhofar rebellion, a small garrison here, with the help of British SAS soldiers, held off a large guerrilla attack in a battle that is still remembered in Oman and in Britain, and the old fort at the edge of town is where the fighting took place. The tomb of Mohammed bin Ali, a scholar of the twelfth century who is revered as a saint, lies in the town and draws visitors.

The road from Salalah follows the coast, passing Taqah, a small town with an old castle, and Khor Rori, an ancient port site, with a ruined city beside a lagoon that was an important frankincense harbour more than two thousand years ago. It is an easy, fast ride on good tarmac, with the sea on one side and the mountains on the other, and it is a good way to end a day. In the khareef the mountains are green and often hidden in cloud, and the temperature drops, while in the rest of the year the sun is strong and the sea breeze is welcome.

Fuel is easiest in Salalah, and a filling station may be found at Taqah, so make sure you have enough before heading out. In Mirbat, small cafes serve tea, simple meals and fresh fish. Watch for camels on the road, particularly in the evening, and take care on the roundabouts, where sand collects. A walk on the beach at sunset, with the boats drawn up and the call to prayer drifting across the water, is a fine way to finish the ride.
t.cuesta del obispo@-25.2,-65.8:
The Cuesta del Obispo is one of the great roads of northern Argentina, a gravel and tarmac climb that crosses the Sierra del Obispo between Salta and the Calchaquí valleys. The summit, called Piedra del Molino, is at 3,348 metres, high enough to feel the thin air, and the views are enormous. The road is named after a bishop of Salta who is said to have crossed here, and the name has lasted longer than his story.

It climbs from the green, wooded valley of Chicoana in a series of tight switchbacks, passing through cloud forest and then into drier, rockier country where the vegetation shrinks to scrub and bunch grass. Higher up, it enters the Los Cardones National Park, where huge candelabra cactus, the cardones that give the park its name, stand on the slopes like sentinels, some of them hundreds of years old. The light at this altitude is clear and hard, and the colours of the rocks, red, orange and ochre, are extraordinary.

Beyond the summit lies the Recta del Tin Tin, a perfectly straight road of about nineteen kilometres across a high, flat plain, with cardones on both sides and the mountains in the distance. It is one of those places that stays in the mind, a straight line drawn across the sky. Beyond it, the road leads on to Cachi, a whitewashed village with an adobe church and a mountain view.

The surface varies. The route is partly paved and partly gravel, with sections that can be rough, so check conditions before you go, and take it slowly on the switchbacks, where loose stones and sharp turns need respect. Weather changes quickly: fog can fill the pass, and in winter, ice and occasional snow can close the road. Fuel is in Chicoana or Salta, so fill up there, as the Calchaquí valleys have few stations and supplies can run out.

Bring warm clothes, water and a bit of patience for the altitude. Go slowly, stop often, and enjoy a road that feels like the top of the world.
t.molinos@-25.4,-66.3:
Molinos sits at the bottom of a dry, wide valley in the province of Salta, about two thousand metres above the sea, with the Calchaquí mountains standing around it in bands of rust and ochre. The river that made the valley is mostly a braid of stones for most of the year, and the green is confined to a thin ribbon of poplars, vineyards and walled fields along it. Cachí is the nearest proper settlement to the north, roughly forty kilometres off, and Cafayate lies a long day's gentle riding to the south.

The village is built around its church, San Pedro Nolasco, a low whitewashed building of adobe with a bell tower and a roof that uses the wood of the local cardón cactus, which is lighter and tougher than it sounds. Next door stands the old hacienda, once the property of the last Spanish governor of Salta, Nicolás Severo de Isasmendi, and local tradition says his remains rest in the church. The hacienda is now a hotel, which tells you the sort of village this is: a handful of streets, a plaza, a few empanada kitchens, and nobody in a hurry.

The riding along Ruta 40 here is the point of the trip. The road follows the valley floor and drops into dry washes, crosses the odd cattle grid, and climbs onto benches from which you can see twenty kilometres of the same colours repeating. Surfaces change, and so does their condition after the summer rains, so look at the road a long way ahead and keep your speed honest on gravel. Sand collects in the corners. Wind picks up in the afternoon and carries dust, so the best light and calmest air come in the morning, and in the cool months of the southern winter the days are crisp, sunny and cold at dawn.

A few kilometres out, high vineyards climb the slopes. Grapes at this altitude, like torrontés and malbec, ripen under strong ultraviolet light and cold nights, and a wine tasting room in the valley is a better excuse for a pause than most. Do not count on the village for fuel; Cachí and Cafayate are the places where you should fill the tank properly, and a rider with a spare litre in a bottle sleeps better on this road. Carry water too. The air is dry enough that you will drink more than you think, and a stop at Molinos in the shade of the plaza trees, with a pastry and strong coffee, is simply the way to take the altitude gently before the road drops south again.
t.stratford@-39.3,174.3:
Stratford has a clock tower that plays Shakespeare, and the whole town has leant into the joke. Its streets carry names such as Juliet, Romeo and Portia, and the glockenspiel on the tower acts out scenes from Romeo and Juliet several times a day. It is a farming town of a few thousand people on the eastern flank of Mount Taranaki, in the rolling dairy country of the North Island's west, and it is an easy place to like.

The mountain is the star. Taranaki, also called Mount Egmont, is a nearly perfect volcanic cone rising to about 2,500 metres from a plain with nothing else around, and it dominates the skyline for miles. In Māori tradition, the mountain once stood with the other volcanoes in the middle of the island, but lost a fight over a woman and fled west to the coast. When the cloud lifts, which is not as often as you would like, the snow-capped summit is a magnificent sight. A road climbs to the Dawson Falls and the lodge on the mountain's south-eastern side.

For riders, Stratford is the start of the Forgotten World Highway, State Highway 43, which runs about 150 kilometres to Taumarunui through very remote hill country. The road is a long, steady sequence of bends over a dozen saddles, through gorges and bush, with little traffic. About a dozen kilometres of it is unsealed, through the Tangarakau Gorge, and loose gravel needs care. It passes the old Moki Tunnel, a hand-cut hole in the hillside, and Whangamomona, a hamlet that declared itself a republic in 1989 and holds a celebratory day every other year. The pub there is a popular stop.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Stratford has stations and shops, but the next dependable fuel is a long way off at Taumarunui, so fill up before leaving and keep a margin. Hawera, about twenty-eight kilometres to the south, is the larger town in the area. Bring food, water and layers, since the weather can change quickly in the hills, with mist and rain common on the western side.

Pick a fine day for the highway. It rewards patience with some of the quietest and most scenic riding in the country.
t.mughsail@16.9,53.8:
At Mughsail the mountains of southern Oman run straight into the Arabian Sea and stop. The cliffs here, pale and weather-stained, drop in sheer walls to a long beach of pale sand, and in the middle of the rock you will find the blowholes, natural chimneys through which the sea is forced up and sprays into the air. Sunset on the sand, with the cliffs glowing orange and the waves crashing at your feet, is a reward for a very long ride.
t.auckland@-36.8,174.8:

t.alemania@-25.6,-65.6:

t.amphitheatre@-25.8,-65.7:

Along the road, different formations have names such as the Toad, the Friars and the Obelisk, and the tourist buses stop at each.

t.devils throat@-25.8,-65.7:

t.tehran@35.7,51.4:
Tehran sits against the Alborz mountains like a city pressed up to a wall, and from the northern suburbs you can look up at snow peaks while the traffic below never seems to stop. It is a huge place, with several million people in the city and many more in the metropolitan area, and Damavand, the volcanic cone that is the highest peak in the Middle East at about 5,600 metres, can be seen on clear days. The north is wealthier and greener; the south is older, dustier and busier. It is not a city for relaxed riding: lanes are suggestions, motorbikes slip through everything, and the pollution can be harsh.

For the Chalus road, though, leaving Tehran is the first test and a good one. You head north toward the mountains, and the route climbs steadily through the Alborz foothills and up to a high crossing, where the road enters a long tunnel before dropping toward the Caspian Sea. The Chalus road is one of the most famous mountain routes in Iran, built in the 1930s under Reza Shah, and it remains a popular weekend run for Tehranis who want to escape the heat and reach the sea.

Weather is the main point. In summer, the north of Tehran is warm and dry, while the road over the mountains can be cool, foggy and busy. In winter, snow and ice close sections or require chains. The best times are late spring and early autumn, and early starts to avoid the Friday traffic, when it seems half the capital drives to the Caspian. Fuel is easy in Tehran and along the main routes, and petrol is cheap by international standards, though rules for foreign vehicles and travellers vary, so check before you go.

Take time for breakfast before leaving: warm barbari bread, cheese, walnuts, sweet tea and a little jam is the classic combination. Tehran has fine museums and gardens if you have a free morning, including the Golestan Palace and the Grand Bazaar. But for a rider, the real city is the one you leave behind, climbing into cool air and a world of mountains and mist.
t.karaj@35.8,50.9:
Karaj is where Tehran's sprawl runs out of road and the mountains begin, a city of well over a million people on the southern slopes of the Alborz. It is the capital of Alborz province, a commuter and industrial city with wide boulevards, apartment blocks and a long list of traffic jams, and for a rider heading north it is mostly a place to get through rather than linger in. Do the necessary things here, fill the tank, eat, check the bike, and then point the front wheel at the hills.

The reason for coming is the road. The route north from Karaj towards Chalus, known simply as the Chalus Road, is one of the great mountain highways of Iran, built in the 1930s to link the capital to the Caspian shore, and it climbs through the Alborz in a succession of bends, tunnels and gorges. Within a few kilometres of leaving the city, the landscape changes completely. You pass the Amir Kabir dam and its long reservoir, where the water is a surprising turquoise against the bare hills, and the road starts to coil upward past villages, orchards and roadside stalls selling local fruit and honey.

Traffic is the main hazard. On weekends and holidays the Chalus Road fills with cars from Tehran heading for the Caspian, and the queues can be long and the driving aggressive. Weekdays and early mornings are much calmer. The road itself is generally well surfaced and busy with trucks, so patience is as useful as skill, and care on blind corners and in tunnels is essential. Authorities sometimes manage the flow, and it pays to ask locally about conditions.

Fuel is no problem in Karaj, where stations are frequent, and the same is true of food. There are bakeries, kebab restaurants and tea houses along the main roads, and the traditional dish of the area, a simple grilled meat with rice and flatbread, is as satisfying here as anywhere. Bring cash and check the current rules on fuel purchase for foreign vehicles, which have changed over the years.

Karaj's own history is a little overshadowed by the capital next door, but it grew rapidly in the twentieth century as Tehran expanded. The best time to ride out is spring or autumn, when the hills are clear and the air is clean, and an early start gets you past the worst of the traffic.
t.kandovan pass@36.2,51.3:
Kandovan Pass is the high point of the Chalus Road, a saddle in the Alborz mountains at about 2,700 metres where the road crosses the watershed between the dry plateau of the Iranian interior and the damp forests that face the Caspian Sea. This is not the Kandovan of the famous rock-cut cave houses in the north-west, which is a different place entirely. Here the name belongs to a pass and a tunnel, and the importance is in what happens on either side.

The south side is open and sparse, with grey slopes and sheep tracks, and the road climbs in bends from the Karaj valley. The north side is a different world, with the cloud pouring over the crest and falling into green forest. A tunnel carries the main road through the ridge, and the old pass road, which twists over the top, is a rewarding diversion for those who want a slower and more scenic route if it is open. The contrast between the dry and the wet is one of the great experiences of riding in this country, and it can happen within a few minutes.

In summer, the pass is often a relief from the heat of the plateau, and cloud rolling in from the Caspian lets you feel the temperature drop. Gusts, rain and sudden fog are all normal. Watch for trucks which grind up and then come down fast with hot brakes, particularly on the descent.

Traffic also varies. During holidays and weekends, thousands of cars come this way, and the queues at the tunnel can be long. If you can, choose a weekday for the crossing.

Fill in Karaj before leaving, and plan to refuel again on the Caspian side, in Chalus or the towns along the coast. At the top and in the villages, you can usually find tea, bread, and simple food from roadside stalls, but the choices thin out as you climb, so do not rely on them.

Once through, the descent through beech forest towards Chalus is a pleasure, with long bends, damp air and the smell of leaves, and the Caspian waiting at the bottom.
t.chalus@36.7,51.4:
Chalus is the Caspian side of the mountain, and the change you feel on arrival is almost physical. After the dry heights of the Alborz, the air thickens and turns humid, the hillsides are covered in green forest, and rice paddies and tea plantations appear on the lowlands. The town has about seventy thousand people, with Nowshahr only a few kilometres to the east, and it sits on a narrow coastal plain between the mountains and the sea. It is a holiday town for Iranians, who flock here in the summer to swim and eat grilled fish.
