After the long climb from Tehran and the tunnel at the top, it descends through the beautiful Chalus valley, with the river running beside you in a gorge. The corners tighten, the forest closes in, and the temperature rises. Fog is common near the top and rain is frequent on the northern side, since the mountains catch the moisture from the sea. The surface is mostly good but can be slick, and heavy trucks and weekend traffic are a constant. Take care on the descent, and do not follow the locals in their overtaking.

The Caspian is the world's largest inland body of water, and it is not a normal sea: it is salty but much less than the ocean, and it is home to sturgeon, whose roe is the famous caviar. The coastal plain grows tea, rice and citrus, and the forests of the Hyrcanian region, which stretch along these slopes, are an ancient survivor of the broadleaf forests that covered the area millions of years ago. They are a UNESCO World Heritage listing for good reason.

For fuel and food, Chalus has everything: pumps, restaurants, hotels. Kebab is a staple, but here you should try the local specialities: fish, pomegranate-walnut stew called fesenjan, and rice dishes with herbs. Evening on the shore is relaxed, with families walking and eating ice cream. If you can, stay overnight and enjoy the green, wet, slow-moving world on the north side of the mountain.
t.cuesta del obispo@-25.2,-65.9:
The Cuesta del Obispo is one of the great mountain roads of northwest Argentina, a winding climb from the green valleys near Salta to a high pass at about 3,350 metres, followed by a descent into the dry Calchaquí valley. The name means the Bishop's Slope, and it recalls a bishop of the colonial church. The scenery is magnificent, with steep green hillsides covered in cloud forest at the bottom, bare rock and golden grass at the top, and then the red, dry valley on the far side.

The ascent, on Ruta 33, is a long series of hairpins and bends, with views that open out at every turn. Much of the road is gravel, with sections of rough surface, loose stones and the odd rock fall, so ride with care and keep to the inside on blind bends. Fog is common on the climb, especially in the afternoon, and it can reduce visibility to a few metres. In summer, the rainy season, storms and landslides may close the road, so check conditions before you set out. The best season is April to October, when the weather is dry and clear.

At the summit, the pass is marked by a stone monument at a place known as Piedra del Molino, and the view across the valley is superb. Beyond lies the Los Cardones National Park, named after the giant cacti that stand like candelabras on the hillsides, some of them many centuries old. The long straight known as the Recta del Tin Tin, which crosses the valley floor, is one of the most photographed sections of road in Argentina. The wind here can be strong, and the sun is fierce.

Fill the tank in Salta before leaving, and carry water and warm clothes. At Cachí, a pretty village of whitewashed adobe houses and a small church, you can stop for lunch, with regional food such as empanadas salteñas and locro, a thick maize and meat stew. The riding is demanding, but the setting is among the most beautiful you will find.
t.quebrada de las conchas@-26.0,-65.7:
The Quebrada de las Conchas is a canyon cut by the Río de las Conchas through the red rock of the Calchaquí valleys, in Salta province, and the road that follows it, Ruta 68, is one of the great scenic rides in Argentina. The rock is sedimentary, laid down in ancient seas and lakes and later uplifted and eroded by wind and water, so that it stands in curved layers of red, orange, pink and ochre. Over time, the elements have carved it into shapes that have been given names: the Devil's Throat, a narrow gorge, the Amphitheatre, a vast natural bowl with extraordinary acoustics, and the Castles, a row of jagged towers.

The ride from Salta to Cafayate, through the canyon, is smooth and enjoyable. The road is paved and in good condition, with long, curving bends, gentle gradients and plenty of viewpoints where you can pull off. It follows the dry riverbed, crossing it on small bridges, and the colours change with the light, with the best views in the early morning and late afternoon. Traffic is moderate, with tour buses and cars, and the main hazards are the occasional rock on the road after a storm and strong winds in the afternoon. In summer, the rains can bring flash floods and landslides, so check conditions.

Cafayate, about twenty-six kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels. It is also the centre of one of the highest wine regions in the world, famous for its Torrontés, a fragrant white wine that suits the dry heat. Many bodegas offer tastings, and a glass of cold white after a day in the canyon is a fine reward.

The landscape feels like a Western film set, with dusty light, red cliffs and cardón cacti on the slopes. Condors sometimes ride the air above, and in the quiet side canyons you can hear the sound of your own boots. Walk a few metres from the road at one of the viewpoints, touch the warm rock, and listen to the wind carry sand over the stones. It is a place where geology becomes visible, and a ride that is very hard to forget.
t.sa adossaltaneh@36.3,50.0:
Qazvin was once a capital, which is a surprising thing to find out as you roll into a busy Iranian provincial city at the foot of the Alborz. In the sixteenth century the Safavid shahs moved their court here, and it stayed the capital for several decades until Shah Abbas shifted it to Isfahan, so the town still carries traces of that grandeur, with a royal mosque, a pavilion called Chehel Sotun, and a gate that once guarded the palace. The caravanserai of Saʿadossaltaneh comes from a later age, the Qajar era of the nineteenth century, and is one of the best-preserved in the country.

A caravanserai was a roadside inn for merchants, a walled courtyard with rooms around it, stables for the animals and space to unload goods for the night. This one has been restored and fits into the bazaar area, with brick arches, passages and courtyards that feel more like an indoor street than a hotel. Qazvin sat on the road between Tehran and the Caspian and the west, so traffic through here was heavy, and there is still a sense in the old centre that people are on their way somewhere else and have stopped for tea.

The approach by road is not subtle. You come in on a motorway or busy trunk road from Tehran, surrounded by trucks and shared taxis, and the only trick is patience; Iranian traffic is fast, fluid and not especially concerned with lane markings. Once you are in the old town, the streets narrow and slow down, and it is a good place to park and walk. Further north the road climbs into the Alborz toward Alamut, the valley of the old Assassin fortresses, and that is where the riding gets properly interesting, with long climbs, hairpins and cold air.

Qazvin is large enough that fuel is plentiful, and its cafes and sweet shops are good places to rest before the mountains. Spring and autumn are comfortable; winter brings snow on the heights and sharp mornings. Be courteous with photography inside the bazaar and the caravanserai, and ask before pointing a camera at anyone who is working.
t.parand@35.5,51.0:
Parand is not a place most people would call romantic. It sits in the flat country south-west of Tehran, a new-town sprawl of apartment blocks, factories and warehouses, a few kilometres from the international airport, and the main reason to stop is the railway. The Trans-Iranian Railway, built in the 1930s under Reza Shah, runs through this region, and it was a serious feat of engineering in its day, linking the Caspian Sea in the north with the Persian Gulf in the south across more than a thousand kilometres.

The route is famous for what lies elsewhere along it. It crosses the Alborz and the Zagros ranges through some of the most difficult terrain in the Middle East, with hundreds of bridges and tunnels, spirals, viaducts and cuttings, many designed by foreign engineers from Germany, Austria, Italy and other countries. The whole line was listed as a World Heritage site in 2021. Down here on the plain, the interest is quieter: you are looking at the line where it was relatively easy to build, and you can think about the mountains that come later.

Practically, this is an urban ride, and it should be planned that way. The roads around Parand and Robat Karim are wide and fast, shared with heavy goods vehicles, airport traffic and commuters, with little scenery and a fair amount of dust. Early morning, before the heat and the traffic build, is the best time, and Friday, the Iranian weekend, is quieter than other days. If you want to get out to the countryside, the Qom road to the south and the old road to Saveh give you broader landscapes and more distance between the buildings.

Fuel is not a problem here, because the area is full of stations, and Robat Karim, about ten kilometres away, has shops and food. You will not find tourist cafes, but you will find sandwich shops, bakeries and tea stalls, and people generally will be curious about a foreign rider. Keep your documents with you, ride defensively, and treat the plain as a place to get through rather than a destination.
t.alamut castle@36.4,50.6:
The Alamut valley lies in the Alborz mountains of northern Iran, in the province of Qazvin, a long, narrow trench of barley fields and walnut trees between steep slopes. The castle stands on a narrow rock spur at around two thousand metres, about the height of a small mountain, and the climb up from the valley is steep and loose, with a few steps cut in the rock. The nearest towns are well away, so reaching it takes a day from Qazvin.

Alamut was the stronghold of the Nizari Ismailis, a branch of Shia Islam, and its first master, Hassan-i Sabbah, took the castle in 1090 and ruled a network of mountain fortresses from it for more than thirty years. Later European writers, including accounts attributed to Marco Polo, turned the story into a legend of drugged young men who were taken to a secret garden and sent out to kill, giving us the word assassin. Historians doubt much of that tale. What is certain is that Alamut was an important centre of learning with a famed library, and that in 1256 the Mongol army under Hulagu besieged it, and the Ismaili ruler surrendered. The Mongols destroyed the castle and much of the library, so little remains but foundations, a few walls, cisterns and a spectacular view over the valley.

The ride is the best part of the visit. From Qazvin the road goes north through a dry plain and climbs into the Alborz by way of the Moalem Kalayeh road, a mountain route with hairpins and long climbs through bare slopes, opening into the green Alamut valley with the lake of Ovan nearby. Roads here can be narrow, with sheer drops, loose gravel and rockfalls, especially after snow or heavy rain. The altitude means that nights are cold even in summer, and snow can close routes from late autumn through spring. The best months are May, June and September.

Fill the tank before you leave Qazvin, a city of several hundred thousand, since stations in the valley are few. Villages sell fresh bread, yoghurt and honey, and you can find simple guesthouses. Carry water and sun protection for the climb, and check conditions with local people before you set out.
t.vaz@36.3,52.1:
The Alborz mountains form a wall between the Caspian coast and the Iranian plateau, and on the northern face the rain makes everything green. The Hyrcanian forests, which run in a belt along the Caspian side, are among the oldest broadleaf forests in the world, a survivor of the great forests that once covered the northern hemisphere before the ice ages, and UNESCO listed them in 2019. They hold Caspian beech, oak, hornbeam and the Persian ironwood, with an undergrowth of ferns, and in the mist the effect is that of an enchanted wood. Brown bears, wolves, lynx and the rare Persian leopard live in these forests, though a visitor is unlikely to see them.

Vaz is a village in the forested foothills south-west of the town of Amol, in Mazandaran, and Alimestan, the other name on this ride, lies in the same wooded range. The nearest city on the map is Amol, about thirty kilometres away. Amol is the gateway to the Haraz road, one of the most spectacular mountain roads in Iran, which climbs from the Caspian plain to the highlands and winds past Mount Damavand, a snow-capped volcanic cone of 5,610 metres and the highest peak in Iran and the highest volcano in Asia. The road is crowded at weekends with holidaymakers from Tehran.

The riding in the Alborz is a full experience. The Haraz road is a long series of hairpins and bends, climbing through forest and then bare mountain, with tunnels, cliffs and fast-flowing rivers. Weather changes quickly, with fog and rain on the north side and bright sun on the south. Landslides and roadworks are common, and heavy traffic of trucks and buses makes passing difficult. The surface can be rough.

Conditions for foreign riders vary, so check the rules before you go. Amol has fuel and everything else, and the villages have small shops and tea houses. In the forest villages, you may be offered tea and local honey. Late spring and early autumn are the best times. Winter brings snow and ice to the high roads.
t.segment portal del inca rio de la sal@-2:
A long way up in the Atacama, where the desert climbs into the high Andes of northern Chile, a worn path crosses the landscape between a place called the Portal del Inca and the Río de la Sal, the salt river. It is a segment of the Qhapaq Ñan, the great network of Inca roads, which UNESCO listed in 2014 across six countries. In Chile the road went south from the Inca heartland, crossing passes of over four thousand metres to reach the valleys of Copiapó and beyond, and traces of it survive in the dry air with striking clarity: stone markers, small shelters and the line of the trail itself.

The setting is remote and dramatic. The salt flats of the Maricunga region lie at around three and a half thousand metres, with flamingos in the shallow lagoons, vicuñas grazing on the sparse grass, and volcanoes towering over them, among them Ojos del Salado, at nearly seven thousand metres, the highest volcano in the world. The sky is a deep, dark blue and the air is dry and thin, with strong winds and brilliant sunlight. Nights are bitterly cold, even in summer.

This is a harsh place for motorcycles, with the main route being a mix of gravel and broken tarmac, and the altitude saps both engine and rider. Altitude sickness is a real danger, so spend a day or two acclimatising in Copiapó or on the way up, drink water and avoid heavy exertion. Winter storms can close the passes, and in summer a rain storm in the Andes can flood the dry watercourses. The best months are generally from November to April, but weather on the high plateau is unpredictable, and a warm layer and a windproof jacket are essential.

Copiapó, the regional city on the desert coast side, is the last reliable place to fill the tank and buy supplies, and you must bring reserve fuel, water, food and a repair kit of your own. Tell someone your plans, since mobile phone coverage is almost nonexistent, and consider travelling in company. For those who go well prepared, the reward is silence, space and a feeling of walking, or riding, on a road that has been used for six hundred years.
t.abr@36.8,54.9:
Abr means cloud in Persian, and the name tells you exactly what the forest does. On the northern flank of the Alborz mountains, moist air from the Caspian Sea rolls in and settles over the ridges, and the woods of Abr are often wrapped in a cold, wet mist, a green world that feels a thousand kilometres from the desert plateau of central Iran. It is the same range that shields the plateau from rain, so within a few hours you can pass from sparse, sun-baked hills to dripping forest, a contrast that startles anyone who has crossed it.

The village of Abr lies in the province of Semnan, near the town of Shahroud, which sits on the old Khorasan Road, the great east-west highway that carried silk and spices from China to the Mediterranean. Nearby is Bastam, where the ninth-century mystic Bayazid Bastami is buried, and where Mongol-era builders added a shrine and a mosque. The road between Shahroud and the Caspian provinces climbs through the mountains in a series of long switchbacks, with views over the folds of the range and a feeling of travelling between worlds.

The forest is part of the broader Hyrcanian forests, which UNESCO listed in 2019, a belt of ancient broadleaf woodland that stretches along the Caspian coast. Oak, hornbeam, beech and the Persian ironwood give the forest its character, and in autumn it turns copper and gold. Leopards live in these mountains, though you are very unlikely to see one, and brown bears, wild boar and roe deer are also found.

For a rider, the mountain roads are spectacular but demanding, with tight bends, steep climbs, trucks in the lower sections and heavy fog higher up. Conditions change fast, and in winter snow can close the passes. Late spring and autumn are the best seasons. Always check local conditions, since road surfaces and access may vary.

Azadshahr, thirty-six kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town, with fuel and food. Qarnabad, a village, has few services. Fill the tank before you climb, and carry warm clothing and water.
t.boola@36.1,53.4:
Boola is a name that appears on the map with nothing around it, and that is a fair description of this stretch of the Alborz. The coordinates lie on the high, dry southern flank of the range, near the border between Semnan and Mazandaran provinces, where the mountains drop north to the Caspian and south to the Iranian plateau. There are few villages, little traffic and almost no services, and the sense of space is considerable.

The label also names Bagh-e Abbasabad, the Abbasabad Garden, which belongs to a different world. It lies on the Mazandaran side, in the lowlands near Behshahr, and was laid out for Shah Abbas I, the Safavid ruler who loved this green Caspian region and built roads, bridges and a palace here in the early seventeenth century. It is one of the Persian Gardens that UNESCO listed in 2011, a design in which water, shade and geometry create an earthly paradise, and the word paradise comes from an old Persian term for an enclosed garden.

The contrast between the two sides of the Alborz is the great theme of any journey here. On the southern side the slopes are dry, rocky and covered with thorny scrub, while on the northern side, just a few kilometres away, thick forest drips with moisture and the air smells of damp leaves. The mountains hold back the clouds, so the north gets the rain and the south gets the sun. Passes cross the crest by tunnels and switchbacks, and the weather on top can change in minutes, with mist, snow and fierce wind.

Roads here are demanding. They are steep, narrow and often in poor repair, with trucks grinding up the grades and long stretches without a village. Winter snow can close the passes, and spring brings rock falls and mud. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, when the days are clear and the roads are clear.

Services are scarce. No sizeable town lies close, so fill the tank and carry water, food and warm clothing. Check local advice on conditions and access before you set off.
t.trans iranian railway@35.7,51.4:
Tehran's railway station is an odd place to begin a motorcycle ride, but it makes sense once you know what it stands for. The Trans-Iranian Railway was the great project of Reza Shah, the officer who became monarch in the 1920s and wanted a modern country stitched together by steel. It ran from the Caspian Sea in the north to the Persian Gulf in the south, cutting through the Alborz and the Zagros mountains on a staggering number of bridges and tunnels, and it was finished in 1938. The route was chosen partly so that Iran would not depend on the old lines of the Russians and British, and partly because it simply could be done by Iranian labour with foreign engineers, which was a point of national pride.

Strangely, the railway has a second life in the story of the Second World War. Within a few years the Allies were using it to push supplies north to the Soviet Union, and the line carried an enormous tonnage along what became known as the Persian Corridor. When people say Iran was always a crossroads, this is the twentieth-century proof.

Now the riding. Tehran is a city of seven million at the foot of the Alborz, and the station sits in the southern part of the centre, a few kilometres from the old bazaar. Traffic is dense, lane markings are treated as suggestions, and motorcycles filter through everything, so keep your mirrors honest and your eyes up. Fuel is cheap and plentiful, and every neighbourhood has a pump, with smaller towns such as Shahrak-e Emam Hasan just beyond the ring road. The reward comes when you leave. On a clear morning after rain, Mount Damavand, a perfect snow-streaked cone of more than five thousand metres, floats above the northern haze, and the roads that climb into the Alborz are wonderful.

Food is easy here and I would take advantage of it before heading out. A plate of kebab with grilled tomato and flat bread, or a bowl of thick abgusht, will carry you a long way, and tea turns up unasked.

A quiet word on timing: the city is at its most rideable early on Friday, the day of rest, when the streets empty out and you can finally see the old buildings rather than the bumper in front of you.
t.jahan nama@36.7,54.4:
Gorgan lies where northern Iran stops being desert-minded and turns green, on the plain between the Caspian shore and the Alborz range. The coordinates for Jahan Nama fall in the foothills a short way out of the city, at the point where the plain starts to crumple into forested ridges, and I should be straight about it: I do not know the particular building or viewpoint behind the name, so I will describe the country instead of inventing a tour. It is a part of Iran that surprises people who expect only dust and domes.

The forests here belong to the Hyrcanian belt, a strip of ancient broadleaf woodland along the southern Caspian that survived the ice ages and earned UNESCO status in 2019. Oak, hornbeam, beech and the famous Persian ironwood grow thickly, and in autumn the hillsides go orange and copper while the air turns damp and mushroomy. Rain comes off the Caspian, and mist hangs in the valleys, so the light is soft and the smell is of wet leaves rather than the dry spice most people imagine for Iran.

Gorgan itself is a big city of over two hundred thousand, so fuel, food, banks and a bed are no problem, and the bazaar area has the usual kebabs, rice with fish from the sea and sour pomegranate sauces from the north. Qarnabad, the next small place, is a village with a few shops. If you are planning to ride beyond the main roads, fill the tank in Gorgan first, and carry a map or offline navigation since signs may be only in Persian.

The roads climbing from the plain are narrow and twisty, shaded by trees and often damp, with moss on the edges and leaves on the tarmac, and local drivers tend to treat the middle of the road as their own. Lorries rumble down from the hills with timber, and motorbikes of the small Iranian kind buzz along every lane. Take care in rain, when the surface can be slick, and be ready for sudden mist.

History is close at hand. The Sasanian-era Gorgan Wall, one of the longest ancient defensive barriers in the world, once ran across the plain here, and the Turkmen steppe to the north has a very different culture of horses and carpets. The nearby Golestan National Park is among the oldest in the country, and spring and early summer are the kindest seasons to be here.
t.golestan palace@35.7,51.4:
The Golestan Palace sits in the middle of Tehran, behind high walls, and the first impression on stepping in is how quiet it is. A city of many millions presses against the gates, but inside the gardens there are fountains, tiled pavilions, shaded paths and the smell of damp earth and roses. The complex grew over the Qajar dynasty in the nineteenth century, though its origins go back to the Safavid citadel. It is where the Qajar kings held court, received foreign envoys and amassed a collection of gifts, and UNESCO listed it in 2013.

The buildings show a fascinating mix of influences. Persian tilework, mirrors cut into thousands of fragments for the famous Hall of Mirrors, European paintings, crystal chandeliers and carved wooden screens sit together. The marble throne, the Takht-e Marmar, stands on a terrace overlooking the garden, and the palace museum displays royal gifts, carpets, and objects. Naser al-Din Shah, who travelled to Europe and returned full of ideas, shaped much of what you see, including the photographic studio, as he was an enthusiastic early photographer.

As for riding, Tehran is a challenge. The traffic is dense, drivers and motorcyclists weave between lanes, and motorbikes of every size mix in a loose flow. Air pollution can be heavy, particularly in winter when a temperature inversion traps smog against the mountains. The best approach is to move early, stay alert, and avoid rush hours, and parking near the bazaar is difficult. Many visitors prefer to use the metro for the last part of the journey and leave the bike somewhere safe.

The nearest large amenities are all in the city, which has fuel, food and hotels in abundance, though note that fuel purchases may involve local rules and cards, so ask. Parand, to the south-west, is a smaller satellite town where the ride begins, but the palace itself belongs to old Tehran, near the Grand Bazaar, where you can find dried fruit, saffron, carpets and copperware.

Nearby, the Alborz mountains rise to the north, and on a clear day the snow-covered peaks of Mount Damavand, a volcanic cone over five thousand metres high, can be seen from the heights of the city. Visit in spring or autumn, as summers are scorching and winters cold. Palace opening hours vary and different buildings require separate tickets, so check before going.
t.auckland new zealand@-36.2,174.7:
North of Auckland the coast road thins out and the land becomes greener and wetter, with dairy farms, tidal creeks and little harbours cut deep into the hills. These coordinates fall just north of Warkworth, on the edge of the Mahurangi Peninsula, and the stretch from here to the top of Northland is the beginning of what many riders call the real New Zealand. The ride is the start of a long weekend towards the Bay of Islands.

Warkworth, with a little over three thousand people, is the town that serves the region, set on the Mahurangi River at the head of a long tidal inlet. Early settlers shipped kauri timber from here, and old wharves and stone buildings from that era remain. A short run east lies Matakana, a village that has transformed itself into a magnet for food, art and wine, with a lively Saturday farmers' market. Nearby Kawau Island, reached by ferry, was home to Sir George Grey, one of the early colonial governors, who planted it with exotic animals, and wallabies still hop through the scrub.

The coast here is a series of broad, shallow beaches, such as Omaha and Pakiri, where white sand runs for kilometres and the swell comes in clean from the Pacific. Further north, at Leigh, a marine reserve near Goat Island was established in 1975, the first in the country, and snorkellers can swim among snapper and crayfish that have grown fat and fearless. The sea is cold, even in summer, so bring a wetsuit if you plan to swim.

The riding itself is straightforward. State Highway 1 runs north through the Dome Valley and over the Brynderwyn Hills, with long climbs and open bends, but it carries heavy traffic and many trucks, so the quieter coastal roads are better. Weekend holiday traffic, especially at the start of summer and at Easter, can back up for kilometres. Fuel is available in Warkworth and Wellsford, a smaller town about eighteen kilometres to the north, and you should fill the tank there before heading to the more remote stretches. The weather can change rapidly, with squalls blowing in from the Tasman, so pack waterproofs.
t.northland bay of islands weekend@-36.5,1:
The Kaipara Harbour is one of the biggest natural harbours in the world, a vast, shallow maze of tidal channels, mudflats and mangroves that opens to the Tasman Sea on the west coast north of Auckland, and these coordinates fall near its southern reaches. The region is far less visited than the east coast, and that is part of its attraction. Helensville, the main town, and the hot-spring village of Parakai nearby, lie on the road that leads north from the city.

The area was once the centre of the kauri timber and gum trade. Gum diggers worked the swamps for the fossilised resin, which was exported for varnish, and timber mills along the harbour shipped enormous logs to Auckland and abroad. The kauri forests were felled in a few decades, leaving a landscape of pasture and scrub, and a few survivors still stand in protected reserves. Parakai has thermal pools that draw people from Auckland, with water that comes from deep underground at a comfortable heat, and a soak is a good way to ease sore muscles after a long ride.

The roads here are good for cruising. State Highway 16, the Kaipara Coast Highway, follows the shore, running past oyster farms, old wharves and farmland, with a long series of gentle bends and views across the water. The surface is generally good, but there are logging trucks and the odd slow tractor, so overtake with care. Away from the highway, the back roads are narrower, with gravel patches, tight bends and occasional stock on the road. Wind off the harbour can be strong, and the light at dusk, when the water turns silver and pink, is lovely.

Food is a pleasure on this route. Helensville has bakeries and cafés that serve proper pies, and the smaller villages, including Parakai, have fish and chip shops where the catch is as fresh as you will find. Fuel is available in Helensville and in Wellsford, which has about two thousand people and a larger selection of services, but the stations are fewer than on the main highway, so fill up when you can. In winter the roads can be wet and cold, and the harbour mist can be thick in the early morning, so take care on the bends.
t.rotorua lakes and forest scenic road@-37:
Waiuku is the market town of the Awhitu Peninsula, a blunt thumb of land that pokes north between the Manukau Harbour and the Tasman Sea, south-west of Auckland. These coordinates fall within a couple of kilometres of it, among low green hills, sheep paddocks and clusters of macrocarpa windbreaks. It is a long way from Rotorua, but this is the gentle sort of country that makes a good start to a big day.

The town has seven and a half thousand people and a main street with a few good cafés, a museum in an old building, and a long history tied to the sea. Kauri logs and gum went out from its wharf, and in the 1960s the ironsand that blows up on the west coast beaches was dug and smelted at a steel mill at nearby Glenbrook, which is still the country's only steelworks. The Glenbrook Vintage Railway runs old steam and diesel engines along a few kilometres of track on summer weekends, and children of every age queue for the ride.

The roads run out along the peninsula to Awhitu Regional Park, with farmland on both sides and glimpses of the harbour to the east. The corners are gentle and the surface is mostly sealed, but a few sections are gravel, so a dual-sport bike is handy. Traffic is light, speeds are low and the pace is relaxed. The air smells of grass and salt, and the sheep seem entirely unbothered by passing motorcycles. In late summer the pōhutukawa along the coast burst into red flower, usually around Christmas, giving it the name of the New Zealand Christmas tree.

Swimming is possible on the sheltered side of the peninsula, at sheltered spots on the harbour side, but the west coast, with its surf and rips, is more suited to walkers and surf fishermen than to swimmers. Waiuku has fuel, food and a supermarket, so this is the place to fill the tank before the long road south. The nearest big town, Pukekohe, is about twenty kilometres away. Summer weekends can be busy, with families heading for the beaches, but mid-week is quiet and the road is yours.
Pokeno sits where State Highway 1 meets the old road to Thames, on the edge of the Waikato, and these coordinates lie in the rolling farmland just north of it. The village is known for its bacon and its ice cream, and travellers heading south have been stopping at the roadside for a bite for generations. Beyond it, the road drops to the broad, brown ribbon of the Waikato River, the longest in the country, which rises on the slopes of Mount Ruapehu and flows more than four hundred kilometres to the Tasman.

The district was the front line of the Waikato war of 1863 and 1864, when British and colonial troops fought Māori forces defending their land, and the old redoubts and cemeteries tell a hard story. The Great South Road, which the army built to supply the invasion, still follows much of its line, and the name Mercer, a hamlet on the river, comes from a British officer who died in the campaign. Small museums in the district carry the history for those who want it.

The riding here is more utilitarian than glorious. State Highway 1 is a major freight route, with trucks and holiday traffic, and the back roads through Mangatāwhiri and Mercer are often better. They cross low hills and wetlands, with views of the river and the Hunua Ranges to the north, and the surface is generally good. The wind picks up in the afternoon, and rain can sweep in quickly from the west. In winter, mist lies in the hollows and the farmland turns a deep, sodden green.

Fuel is plentiful at Pokeno, Mercer and Pukekohe, with Pukekohe East about sixteen kilometres away, and the roadside cafés and bakeries are among the best for a quick, cheap bite. Do not miss the chance to stop at one of the bacon sellers. Waiuku is the nearest bigger town to the west, and Te Kauwhata is a pleasant spot on the way to Hamilton. Whichever way you head, bring a spare layer, because the weather in the Waikato can change in minutes.

The shore of the Manukau Harbour south of Auckland is a broad, muddy, tidal landscape, and these coordinates sit on its southern side, among the beaches of the Awhitu Peninsula and Clarks Beach. At low tide the water retreats for kilometres, leaving a vast sheet of sand and mud that is crowded with wading birds, and at high tide it fills the harbour to the brim. The setting sun turns the whole expanse to copper, and across the water the dark line of the Waitākere Ranges, the ride's destination, rises on the northern horizon.

Clarks Beach is a small settlement with a golf club and a long, flat beach, popular with locals who come for fishing and sailing. It is quiet in the winter and busy in the summer, and the tide goes out so far that boats are stranded on the mud. A short distance south, the town of Waiuku offers cafés, shops and fuel. Kariotahi Beach, on the west coast, has black ironsand and heavy surf, and is popular with surfcasters. The ironsand is magnetic, and a magnet drawn through it comes up bristling with fine black grains.

The road between them is a gentle, rolling ribbon, mostly sealed, with a few corners and no steep hills. Traffic is light, the verges are lined with flax and cabbage trees, and the sea is never far off. This is not a road for fast riders, but it suits a relaxed morning, and it offers wide views. The afternoon sea breeze can be strong, and rain squalls often blow across the harbour. Watch for gravel at the junctions and for livestock in the paddocks.

You are about twelve kilometres from Waiuku, the nearest town of any size, which has a population of over seven thousand and enough fuel and food to see you through. There are no stations on the coast. If you want to swim, the sheltered beaches on the harbour side, such as Clarks Beach, are safer than the open west coast, but the mud can be deep and the tides strong, so check the tide times. Summer weekends bring crowds, and spring brings the first warm days and the first flush of wildflowers.
t.east cape long adventure@-37.0,174.5:
Manukau Heads, at the mouth of the Manukau Harbour, is one of the roughest bars in the Southern Hemisphere, and these coordinates sit on the northern shore, near Huia and Whatipu, at the edge of the Waitākere Ranges. The place is a long way from the Mangere airport, but it is only a short trip along a road that winds through bush and down to a lonely sweep of sand. Whatipu is a wide, wild beach backed by high dunes, with caves in the cliffs where dances were once held, and the old lodge near the shore still takes guests.

The Manukau bar was the scene of the worst maritime disaster in New Zealand's history. In 1863 the Royal Navy ship HMS Orpheus, trying to cross the bar in poor conditions, struck a sandbank and broke up with the loss of nearly two hundred lives, and a memorial on the headland records the toll. Today a lighthouse stands on the southern head, and the fierce tide races and breaking waves still demand respect. The beaches are dangerous, with strong rips, and swimming is not advised.

The road to Huia, the village at the end of the line, runs through the forest of the Waitākere Ranges, with steep climbs, tight bends and views of the harbour opening below. It is narrow, damp and often covered in leaves, and it is a road to be taken slowly. The rewards are the sound of tui in the trees and the sight of the bush closing in on both sides. Rain is frequent, and the clouds sit low on the ridges.

Fuel and food are a long way off. Titirangi, on the edge of the ranges, has a station and a few cafés, and the nearest large centre is Mangere, which has everything from supermarkets to repair shops. The ride that starts here heads for the East Cape, a long, remote peninsula on the far side of the island, so it is wise to fill up and eat before you go. A dawn start, with the first light on the sea and the bush quiet and cool, is the best way to begin.
t.east cape long adventure scenic road@-36:
The Hibiscus Coast, north of Auckland's North Shore, is a string of seaside suburbs and beaches that runs from Orewa to the Whangaparāoa Peninsula, and these coordinates fall in the middle of it. It is a comfortable, sunny and rather relaxed place, with a long white-sand beach at Orewa, cafés along the foreshore and a lot of retired people from the city, who like the warm air and the sea. It is also the first place on the northbound road where the city begins to loosen its grip.

Whangaparāoa is a long, narrow peninsula that sticks out into the Hauraki Gulf, and its road runs along the spine to a naval base and a ferry terminal at Gulf Harbour. At its tip lies Shakespear Regional Park, a stretch of grassland, bush and beach that was fenced in 2011 to keep out pests and now supports populations of rare birds, including saddlebacks and takahē. Walkers can follow tracks along the cliffs, with views of Tiritiri Matangi and Little Barrier on the horizon. The area was a major Māori settlement, and its name is said to mean the place of the whale's bay.

The ride follows the coast in a loop through Silverdale, Stillwater and Wainui, with lanes that dip and rise through farms and pockets of bush, and it ends on the beach. The roads are narrow, with gentle bends, and they are busy with cyclists and weekend visitors, so a relaxed pace is best. The surface is good for the most part, with occasional gravel patches and the odd pothole. Sun and sea breezes bring a summery feel for much of the year, and the afternoon light on the water is lovely.

The area is well provided with fuel stations and food stops, with Orewa and Silverdale at the head of the peninsula, and Warkworth about twenty kilometres to the north. Rothesay Bay and Murrays Bay, on the North Shore, are larger, but the traffic there can be heavy. Late summer is the best time, when the sea is warm and the roads are quiet, and in winter the weather can be wet and windy, though the beaches are empty and the light is clean.
t.whangamomona@-39.1,174.7:
There is a republic here, and it takes itself exactly as seriously as it should. In 1989 the folk of Whangamomona, annoyed at a boundary change that moved them from Taranaki into Manawatu-Wanganui, declared independence, and they have kept the joke running ever since. Republic Day is held every other January, and the presidents elected over the years have included a goat and a poodle, which says something about the standard of candidates. A passport stamp from the hotel is the souvenir, and you can reasonably claim to have crossed a border.

The village is tiny, a handful of buildings along State Highway 43, the Forgotten World Highway, which links Stratford in Taranaki to Taumarunui, about 150 kilometres of twisting road through bush and hill farms. The hotel is the heart of the place, a wooden building with a wide veranda, a bar that has seen a lot of dust and a lot of motorcyclists. Mud and rain come with the territory, and the road in this area is steep, winding and tight, passing over saddles with names like Tahora and Strathmore. A stretch of the highway between here and Taumarunui is unsealed, around a dozen kilometres, which is good to know before you book that tight touring schedule.

What you notice about the landscape is that it is both lush and eroded, steep pasture cut by landslips on soft papa mudstone hills, and the whole district is a world of green. The Whangamomona River winds below the village, and the hills around it fold up steeply on every side. Early settlers cleared the hillsides for farms, and many of the farms were later abandoned, hence the Forgotten World. Rail and road builders cut a tunnel through the hills nearby, the Moki Tunnel, and the Tangarakau Gorge section is wild and narrow.

Fuel is the one practical point to take seriously. There is nothing between Stratford and Taumarunui that you can rely upon, so fill at one end and ride the whole length on that tank, with a reserve. Stratford is the usual start, a pleasant town with a view of Mount Taranaki on a clear day. In the hotel you can get a hot meal and a cold drink, and a chat about the road ahead from whoever is behind the bar.

Go slowly, expect rain, and watch for stock on the road. The best days are late spring and autumn, when the hills are green and the traffic light.
t.hobbiton waikato easy ride high point@-3:
This point lies on the Awhitu Peninsula, a long finger of land between the Manukau Harbour and the Tasman Sea, south-west of Auckland. It is a quiet, rolling countryside of farms, scrub and old pine plantations, with a wild western coast of black sand beaches and dunes. The Awhitu Regional Park has a heritage farm, a lighthouse and trails, and it feels a world away from the city, though it is only an hour's drive from it. At the northern tip, the Manukau Heads look across a narrow entrance to the Waitakere Ranges.

The entrance to the Manukau Harbour is one of the most dangerous bars in New Zealand, a shifting maze of sandbanks where the swell from the Tasman meets the tide, and many ships have been wrecked on it. The worst disaster was in 1863, when the British warship HMS Orpheus ran aground on the bar and more than a hundred and eighty of her crew were lost, the worst maritime disaster in the country's history. A lighthouse at the heads, built later in the nineteenth century, guides ships through the entrance, and a memorial recalls the dead.

The peninsula's roads are narrow and winding, mostly sealed but with gravel in places, and they go through a quiet, pastoral landscape of paddocks, hedges and macrocarpa trees. The traffic is very light, and the views over the harbour and out to the Tasman are lovely. Wind is a constant, sometimes strong enough to be a nuisance, and the weather can change in minutes. It is best ridden on a dry day, since wet gravel and sand on the corners are slippery. Take care on blind bends, where farm vehicles and stock trucks may appear.

A small cafe or two operate at weekends, but services are limited. Bring water and a snack. The west coast beaches have strong currents and no lifeguards, so avoid swimming. At sunset, the black sand turns copper, and the sky over the Tasman is full of colour, a fine reward for a ride out to the edge of the land.
t.hobbiton waikato easy ride scenic road@-:
The countryside west of Auckland, around Kumeu and Huapai, is wine country, gently rolling and green, with vineyards, orchards and lifestyle blocks stretching along the old State Highway 16 toward the Kaipara Harbour. It is one of the oldest winemaking regions in New Zealand, and it owes its start to Dalmatian immigrants from Croatia, who came in the late nineteenth century to dig kauri gum in the north and then settled on the land, planting grapes and making wine for their families. Several of the best-known New Zealand wine families have their roots here.

The gum diggers' story is part of the landscape. The great kauri forests of the north were felled in the nineteenth century for timber, and the fossilised resin buried in the ground, kauri gum, was dug out in huge quantities and shipped to make varnish. The work was hard and badly paid, and it left the land scarred and bare, with few trees. To the west, Woodhill Forest, a huge plantation of pine on old sand dunes, now covers part of the country, and offers mountain biking and horse riding trails.

For a rider, the roads here are gentle, with curves through farmland and the occasional steep hill, and the traffic is heavy on the main highway, especially at the weekend when Aucklanders head for the west coast beaches. The quieter side roads through Waimauku and Riverhead are pleasant, with old trees, vineyards and views over the hills. The surface is mostly good, with some patches of rough chip seal, and the weather is mild, with sunshine and showers. Autumn brings gold in the vineyards.

Fuel is available in Kumeu and Huapai, which have stations and shops, and in Helensville to the north. Food options are good, with cafes and restaurants attached to vineyards offering tastings and long lunches, though as a rider you will be best advised to leave the wine for another day. A cold pie from a bakery and a flat white are the standard Kiwi fuel. Respect the speed limits, which are strictly enforced, and keep left. The country smells of cut grass and woodsmoke in the evenings.

The coordinates lie just north of Auckland, in the hills near the village of Puhoi, where the Hibiscus Coast meets the farming country of the Rodney district. It is a land of rolling green hills, small valleys and tidal inlets, with the Hauraki Gulf glittering to the east and the Pacific beyond it. The village of Puhoi itself sits beside a winding, muddy river, in a steep-sided valley, and it has a remarkable origin: it was settled in 1863 by families from Bohemia, in what is now the Czech Republic, one of the most unusual settlements in the country.

The Bohemian pioneers cleared the bush, built houses and a church and held on to their language and customs, and descendants of those families still live in the area. The village hotel, built in 1879, has a collection of memorabilia on its walls and a pleasant garden by the river, and it is a popular stop with riders on the Northland road. A little museum tells the story of the settlers, and the old cemetery has gravestones carved with Bohemian names. It is a charming, quiet place.

Just to the south, Waiwera has hot springs that have drawn visitors for more than a century, and farther down the coast, Orewa has a long, safe beach lined with pohutukawa trees. The motorway north from Auckland is fast and takes you through tunnels under the hills, but the old road through Puhoi is slower and more attractive, with views over the valleys and the glimpse of the sea. Photographs from the viewpoints, looking east across the farmland to the islands in the gulf, are especially good in the soft light of early morning or late afternoon.

For fuel, the towns of Orewa and Silverdale, a short way south, have stations and shops, and Warkworth, to the north, is another good option. Dhofar was the source of frankincense, the resin from a small thorny tree that grows on the arid slopes inland, and for thousands of years it was carried by camel and ship to Egypt, Rome and India. The ruins of Al Baleed, an old port by the sea, and the harbour at Khor Rori are part of the World Heritage listing for the Land of Frankincense. In the souq you can buy the resin and a little burner and smell the city's old trade at first hand. The sultan who ruled Oman for half a century, Qaboos, was born in Salalah, which gives the town a special weight in the country.

The riding is a pleasure with a few cautions. West of town the coast road leads to Mughsail, about forty-five kilometres, where white sand meets black cliffs and blowholes shoot spray high on a rough sea, and the road beyond climbs a dramatic escarpment to the Yemeni border region. East toward Mirbat the road runs through low hills and fishing villages. Camels wander across the road at will, often in the dusk and in the mist of the khareef, when visibility can drop to a few metres, so slow down. Summer afternoons outside the monsoon are fiercely hot, and the best riding is early or late.

Salalah is big enough for every kind of fuel, food and repair, and stations are frequent along the main roads. The seafood is good and fresh, and a glass of fresh coconut water from a roadside stall is a local pleasure. Speed cameras are common, and Omani police are firm about limits.

For about twelve kilometres here the tarmac gives way to gravel, and the road squeezes between steep, bush-covered walls beside the Tangarakau River, in a landscape of papa mudstone, tree ferns and mist. There is no town of any size nearby, and the closest, Waitara, is a long way west, so this is a stretch to approach with a full tank and a plan.

A rider should take it slowly, avoid the middle where stones gather, and watch for logging trucks and oncoming cars. Summer is the best time, and a dry day makes it a delight, while wet weather can turn the clay surface treacherous. Fuel stops are few: fill in Stratford or Taumarunui, and do not rely on the little roadside pubs for petrol.

The highway earns its name from its history. The road follows the line of an old bridle track used by settlers in the late nineteenth century, who struggled to farm the steep, bush-covered land, and many farms were abandoned after the Depression and the land reverted to scrub. At nearby Whangamomona, a tiny village with a historic hotel, locals declared a republic in 1989 after a boundary change, complete with a president, and they hold a festival every second January. Tangarakau itself was once a railway-building settlement, and its name lives on as a ghost town in the forest, a fitting symbol of the forgotten world.

The landscape is rich and green. Podocarp forest, rimu, rata and tawa, cloaks the slopes, and the air smells of damp earth and leaf mould. Native birds, including tui, bellbirds and fantails, flit through the bush, and the river runs cold and clear over papa rock. Glow-worms appear in the dark in damp spots, though this is not a ride to attempt at night.

Carry water, food, a tyre repair kit and warm clothes, since mobile coverage is patchy and help may be slow. Treat the gravel with respect, and enjoy the feeling of riding through a place time has overlooked.

Whangamomona is a village with a population that can be counted on one's fingers and a political history that is considerably larger. In 1988, when regional boundaries were redrawn and the village found itself moved from Taranaki to Manawatu-Wanganui against its wishes, locals shrugged, declared independence and proclaimed the Republic of Whangamomona the following year. Presidents have been elected since then, and they have included a goat and a poodle, with the position taken more seriously by its supporters than its critics might suppose.

The centre of the republic is the Whangamomona Hotel, a wooden pub built in the early twentieth century, which still serves food and drink to travellers and will stamp your passport, for a small fee, with an official republic stamp. The building and the few houses around it are the remains of a once-busy timber and farming settlement, and old photographs inside show the village in its heyday, when the railway was under construction and the hills were being cleared.

The riding to get here is the highlight of the Forgotten World Highway. From Taumarunui the road climbs and falls through hill country, with a series of tight bends, narrow bridges and blind crests, and the surface varies from good tar to patched and broken. Livestock is common on the road, and trucks hauling logs and stock use it. Fog and rain can reduce visibility, and a rider needs to be alert. The reward is a sense of remoteness that is increasingly rare in the North Island.

Food and drink are available at the hotel, which makes this the natural lunch stop, but fuel is not, so make sure your tank was full from Taumarunui and that you have enough to reach Stratford. Accommodation is limited to a few cabins and the hotel, and booking ahead is wise if you want to stay. Mobile coverage is poor or nonexistent. The republic holds a celebration in odd-numbered years, with sheep races, gumboot throwing and a presidential election.

The country is wild and green, with steep, forested hills, deep gorges and farmland cut into the slopes. In the morning, mist lies in the valleys, and the smell of damp earth and ferns is strong. Take your time, and enjoy the quiet.
